words.definition: Deoxyribonucleic acid: a long molecule whose sequence of chemical units carries hereditary information.

structure.text: Initialism for deoxyribonucleic acid. Deoxy- distinguishes its sugar from ribose; DNA names a molecule, not a protein.

words.whatItDoes: Its base sequence can be copied and used to produce functional RNA, transmitting genetic information.
words.commonConfusion: DNA is not made of amino acids.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can different base sequences carry different instructions despite using the same four base types?

words.definition: DNA together with associated proteins that package and regulate genetic material in the nucleus.

structure.text: Chromatin is a material noun; chromosomal describes its organization into chromosomes. Chromatin is not a division stage.

words.whatItDoes: Association with proteins packages DNA and helps regulate access to it.
words.commonConfusion: Chromatin and chromosomes are not different hereditary substances.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can genetic material appear diffuse between divisions but condensed during division?

words.definition: An organized DNA–protein structure. Before copying, it contains one DNA molecule. After copying, it contains two attached copies; when they separate, each is counted as a chromosome.

structure.text: Chromo- relates to colour and -some to body in this historical name. Counting chromosomes still requires centromere and separation rules, not visible shape.

words.whatItDoes: Packaging maintains an organized DNA unit that can be copied and distributed during division.
words.commonConfusion: Replication doubles DNA molecules, not immediately the chromosome count.
words.retrievalPrompt: A cell has six chromosomes before replication. How many chromosomes and DNA molecules follow S phase?

words.definition: A region of DNA whose information contributes to a functional RNA molecule or protein.

structure.text: Gene is the noun; genetic is the adjective. A gene is a DNA region, not the visible trait itself.

words.whatItDoes: Its sequence supplies information for a functional RNA or a protein through gene expression.
words.commonConfusion: Not every gene encodes a protein, and one gene need not determine one whole trait.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is a gene that produces functional RNA still a gene?

words.definition: A defined chromosome position or DNA region used to locate a gene or marker.

structure.text: One locus, several loci. The word identifies a position, not which allele occupies it.

words.whatItDoes: A specified position lets geneticists compare corresponding regions and track inheritance.
words.commonConfusion: A locus is a position, not a particular allele.
words.retrievalPrompt: Two homologues carry different alleles. What stays the same about their loci?

words.definition: Two chromosomes with corresponding gene positions, usually one inherited from each parent; they may carry different versions of the same genes.

structure.text: Pair is the head noun; homologous specifies corresponding chromosomes, not identical alleles.

words.whatItDoes: Corresponding chromosomes pair and segregate during meiosis I, distributing parental chromosome sets.
words.commonConfusion: Homologues need not carry identical DNA sequences.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can homologous chromosomes match in gene position but differ in allele content?

words.definition: One of the two DNA copies of a replicated chromosome, initially joined to its sister at the centromeric region.

structure.text: Sister identifies the replication relationship; chromatid names one copy in a replicated chromosome.

words.whatItDoes: The copied DNA unit remains associated with its sister until the appropriate division separates them.
words.commonConfusion: A sister chromatid is not the same relationship as a maternal–paternal homologue.
words.retrievalPrompt: After sisters separate in mitosis, how should each former chromatid be counted?

words.definition: A chromosome region involved in joining sister chromatids and attaching the chromosome to the cell-division machinery.

structure.text: A whole anatomical name for a chromosome region; centromeric is the adjective. It need not lie at the geometric centre.

words.whatItDoes: It organizes kinetochore assembly and contributes to the chromosome region where sisters remain joined before separation.
words.commonConfusion: A centromere is a chromosome region; a kinetochore is an assembled protein structure.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish the centromere from the structure that attaches spindle microtubules.

words.definition: Having one chromosome set, conventionally written n.

structure.text: Haploid is the chromosome-set term for one set. Pair it with n; do not use it as a synonym for an unduplicated chromosome.

words.whatItDoes: One set supplies one representative of each chromosome type in the stated life-cycle stage.
words.commonConfusion: Haploid does not mean every chromosome is unreplicated.
words.retrievalPrompt: Can a haploid cell contain replicated chromosomes? Explain without changing set number.

words.definition: Having two chromosome sets, conventionally written 2n.

structure.text: Diplo- means double; ploid refers here to chromosome-set number. Diploid means two sets, not necessarily two chromatids per chromosome.

words.whatItDoes: Two sets provide corresponding homologues, normally one set from each parent in the examples studied.
words.commonConfusion: Diploid is not a count of chromatids or an indication that DNA has replicated.
words.retrievalPrompt: A diploid cell completes S phase. Why does it remain diploid?

words.definition: Having more than two complete sets of chromosomes; this differs from gaining or losing only one chromosome.

structure.text: Poly- means many; ploidy concerns chromosome sets. Polyploid does not simply mean replicated DNA.

words.whatItDoes: Additional complete chromosome sets change the number of homologous copies across the genome.
words.commonConfusion: An extra single chromosome is aneuploidy, not a whole extra set.
words.retrievalPrompt: For n = 5, contrast a triploid complement with a diploid complement plus one chromosome.

words.definition: A chromosome other than a sex chromosome in the classification being used.

structure.text: An autosome is distinguished from a sex chromosome. Autosomal is the adjective used in inheritance descriptions.

words.whatItDoes: It carries genes outside the sex-chromosome classification used for that organism.
words.commonConfusion: Autosomal genes can still affect reproductive traits.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does a gene affecting reproduction not automatically lie on a sex chromosome?

words.definition: A chromosome associated with sex determination or sex-linked inheritance in a specified organism.

structure.text: Chromosome is the head noun; sex identifies its role in a sex-determination system, not exclusive inheritance from one parent.

words.whatItDoes: Its transmission can create characteristic inheritance patterns in the specified sex-determination system.
words.commonConfusion: Sex chromosomes carry genes unrelated to sex determination as well.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must an X-linked inheritance problem specify which parent supplies which chromosome?

words.definition: An organized display or description of chromosomes used to examine number and large-scale structure.

structure.text: Karyotype names a chromosome complement or its organized representation; karyotyping is the examination process.

words.whatItDoes: An ordered chromosome display helps identify number changes and sufficiently large structural differences.
words.commonConfusion: A normal-looking karyotype does not exclude a small sequence mutation.
words.retrievalPrompt: What can a karyotype show about trisomy that it may not show about a single-base change?

words.definition: The interphase interval before DNA replication, when a cell grows and carries out normal activity.

structure.text: G means gap; 1 distinguishes the interval before S phase. A gap is not cellular inactivity.

words.whatItDoes: Cells carry out functions and grow before the replication interval.
words.commonConfusion: G1 does not mean the cell has no DNA.
words.retrievalPrompt: Compare DNA amount in G1 with the same cell after S phase.

words.definition: The interphase interval in which DNA is replicated.

structure.text: S stands for synthesis; phase names the cell-cycle interval in which DNA is replicated.

words.whatItDoes: DNA synthesis makes sister copies while chromosome-set number remains unchanged.
words.commonConfusion: S phase is not a nuclear division.
words.retrievalPrompt: Track chromosome count and DNA amount through S phase for a cell with 2n = 8.

words.definition: The interphase interval after DNA replication and before mitosis, including preparation and checks.

structure.text: G means gap; 2 identifies the interval after S phase and before mitosis.

words.whatItDoes: The cell prepares for division after replication and can respond to problems before proceeding.
words.commonConfusion: G2 is not another full round of DNA replication.
words.retrievalPrompt: What has already happened to DNA when a cell enters G2?

words.definition: Copying DNA so that each resulting double-stranded molecule has one original strand and one newly made strand.

structure.text: Replication means copying; DNA specifies the copied molecule. Replication is not the same process as cell division.

words.whatItDoes: Complementary pairing supports copying; each daughter duplex retains one parental strand.
words.commonConfusion: Semiconservative replication does not mean one daughter molecule is wholly old.
words.retrievalPrompt: Label old and new strands in the two molecules after one replication round.

words.definition: A regulatory control point that can delay cell-cycle progression when conditions or molecular events are unsuitable.

structure.text: A compound of check and point: a regulatory decision, not a physical dot on a chromosome.

words.whatItDoes: Regulatory signals can pause progression when prerequisites are not satisfied.
words.commonConfusion: A checkpoint reduces risk but does not guarantee every error is detected.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why might a cell delay division when chromosomes lack suitable spindle attachments?

words.definition: Nuclear division that separates replicated sister chromatids into genetically similar daughter nuclei.

structure.text: Mitosis is the process noun; mitotic is the adjective. Nuclear division is distinct from cytokinesis.

words.whatItDoes: Sister separation distributes corresponding chromosome copies to daughter nuclei.
words.commonConfusion: Mitosis does not halve chromosome-set number in normal diploid growth.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how mitosis can maintain 2n while separating chromatids.

words.definition: Physical division of a cell's cytoplasm into daughter cells.

structure.text: Cyto- relates to cells; -kinesis to movement. Here the complete term means cytoplasmic division, not any cell movement.

words.whatItDoes: Division of cytoplasm partitions the cell into daughter cells after or alongside nuclear division.
words.commonConfusion: Nuclear division and cell division are distinct events.
words.retrievalPrompt: What cellular outcome could occur if nuclei divide but cytokinesis does not?

words.definition: Control of when and whether a cell proceeds through growth, replication and division.

structure.text: Cell cycle identifies the controlled sequence; regulation names control of its progression.

words.whatItDoes: Control mechanisms coordinate replication and division with internal and external conditions.
words.commonConfusion: Fast growth alone does not identify which regulatory mechanism changed.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is uncontrolled division evidence of altered regulation but not proof of one specific mutation?

words.definition: The proportion of observed cells that are in mitosis at a particular time.

structure.text: Mitotic modifies index. This index is a fraction of sampled cells, not the duration of mitosis in minutes.

words.whatItDoes: Dividing the number of mitotic cells by total counted cells gives a snapshot proportion.
words.commonConfusion: A snapshot proportion is not directly a division rate without assumptions.
words.retrievalPrompt: Twenty of 200 cells appear mitotic. Calculate the index and state one limit on interpreting it.

words.definition: A selected subset of observations used to investigate a larger population or process.

structure.text: Sample is both noun and verb; sampled cells are the subset examined rather than the entire population.

words.whatItDoes: Selecting observations makes a larger process investigable while introducing sampling constraints.
words.commonConfusion: A large sample can still be biased.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why might counting only one rapidly dividing region misrepresent an entire tissue?

words.definition: The share of total time occupied by one stage, estimated only under appropriate sampling/model assumptions.

structure.text: Duration is elapsed time; relative makes it a comparison with another interval or the whole cycle.

words.whatItDoes: Under appropriate steady-state sampling assumptions, stage proportions can estimate fractions of cycle time.
words.commonConfusion: The estimate fails when cells accumulate or disappear selectively in a stage.
words.retrievalPrompt: When would a high metaphase count fail to mean metaphase normally lasts longest?

words.definition: An early division stage when chromosomes condense, the spindle forms, and nuclear organization changes.

structure.text: The phase name identifies an early division stage; specify mitotic prophase or prophase I when the distinction matters.

words.whatItDoes: Condensation and spindle development prepare chromosomes for segregation.
words.commonConfusion: Not every dense image establishes prophase without other stage evidence.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which visible features would support prophase rather than interphase?

words.definition: A system of protein fibres that positions and moves chromosomes during cell division.

structure.text: A familiar shape word used for the microtubule apparatus. Spindle fibre is not a chromosome fibre.

words.whatItDoes: Microtubule interactions organize chromosome attachment and movement during division.
words.commonConfusion: Spindle fibres do not copy DNA.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain why replicated chromosomes can still segregate incorrectly if spindle attachment fails.

words.definition: A protein attachment structure at a chromosome’s centromere that connects it to spindle fibres.

structure.text: A whole technical name for the attachment complex; kinetochore and centromere name different structures.

words.whatItDoes: The protein complex links a centromeric region to spindle microtubules for chromosome movement.
words.commonConfusion: The kinetochore is not the entire chromosome or the centromeric DNA itself.
words.retrievalPrompt: What mechanical connection is interrupted by a kinetochore attachment defect?

words.definition: A division stage in which chromosomes align near the middle of the cell with attachments to the spindle.

structure.text: A division-phase name. Adding I or II changes which meiotic division and chromosome arrangement is meant.

words.whatItDoes: Chromosome alignment and attachments position copies for subsequent segregation.
words.commonConfusion: Alignment alone does not show that segregation has already occurred.
words.retrievalPrompt: How would you distinguish a metaphase image from anaphase using chromosome positions?

words.definition: The division stage when separated chromosomes or chromatids move toward opposite poles.

structure.text: A division-phase name; I and II distinguish homolog separation from sister separation in meiosis.

words.whatItDoes: Separation moves the appropriate chromosome units toward opposite poles.
words.commonConfusion: The separated units differ between mitosis and meiosis I.
words.retrievalPrompt: Contrast what moves apart in mitotic anaphase and anaphase I.

words.definition: A late division stage when chromosomes reach the poles and new nuclear organization forms.

structure.text: A division-phase name used for late nuclear reorganization. Telophase does not itself mean cytoplasmic division.

words.whatItDoes: Chromosomes at the poles become enclosed in reorganized daughter nuclei.
words.commonConfusion: Telophase does not necessarily mean cytokinesis has finished.
words.retrievalPrompt: What evidence distinguishes nuclear reformation from completed cell separation?

words.definition: A former sister chromatid counted as a separate chromosome after sister separation.

structure.text: Daughter denotes a descendant unit after separation, not the biological sex of the cell.

words.whatItDoes: After sister separation, each former chromatid is an independently counted chromosome.
words.commonConfusion: Its new count status does not mean new DNA was synthesized at separation.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does the chromosome count within one dividing cell change at anaphase before cytokinesis?

words.definition: The inward pinching of an animal cell membrane during cytokinesis.

structure.text: Furrow is a groove; cleavage specifies division. The phrase names a constriction, not a rigid new wall.

words.whatItDoes: A contractile process draws the animal-cell surface inward, partitioning cytoplasm.
words.commonConfusion: A furrow is not a new plant cell wall.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how inward pinching differs from plant cell-plate formation.

words.definition: A plant-cell structure formed during cytokinesis that develops into new membranes and a separating cell wall.

structure.text: Plate names the developing partition; cell places it in plant-cell cytokinesis rather than in a culture dish.

words.whatItDoes: Vesicle-derived material builds a partition inside the dividing plant cell that develops into the daughter-cell boundary.
words.commonConfusion: The plate does not form by pinching the rigid outer wall inward.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is an internal partition useful during plant cytokinesis?

words.definition: A photograph obtained through a microscope; it records actual observed material rather than a schematic drawing.

structure.text: Photo- refers to light and micro- to small scale; a photomicrograph is a microscope photograph, not a diagram.

words.whatItDoes: It preserves a microscope view that can be measured and interpreted with scale and preparation information.
words.commonConfusion: A photograph still reflects sampling and preparation limits; it is not a labelled ideal diagram.
words.retrievalPrompt: What information would you need before estimating cell size from a photomicrograph?

words.definition: Observations or results used to evaluate a claim, together with their method and limitations.

structure.text: A collective noun for observations used to support a claim. Evidential is the adjective; evidence is not identical to inference.

words.whatItDoes: Observations support or challenge a claim when their methods and alternative interpretations are considered.
words.commonConfusion: A conclusion is not itself an observation.
words.retrievalPrompt: Separate the observation of chromosome alignment from an inference about the division stage.

words.definition: A model run under specified rules to examine how its outcomes change; simulated results are not automatically real observations.

structure.text: Simulation is the model-running process; simulated describes its output, not an observed biological event.

words.whatItDoes: Running explicit rules lets a learner test their consequences under selected conditions.
words.commonConfusion: Agreement with a simulation is not independent empirical confirmation.
words.retrievalPrompt: What real observation would help test a chromosome-separation simulation?

words.definition: Close pairing of homologous chromosomes during meiotic prophase I.

structure.text: Synapsis is the pairing process; synaptic here concerns chromosome pairing, not a neuronal synapse.

words.whatItDoes: Close pairing brings homologous regions together during prophase I, supporting meiotic recombination and segregation.
words.commonConfusion: Synapsis joins homologues, not merely the existing sister pair.
words.retrievalPrompt: How many replicated homologues participate in one synapsed pair?

words.definition: The four-chromatid structure formed when replicated homologous chromosomes pair during meiotic prophase I.

structure.text: Tetra- means four: the paired replicated homologues contain four chromatids, not four homologous chromosomes.

words.whatItDoes: Two replicated homologues place four chromatids together during pairing.
words.commonConfusion: A tetrad has four chromatids but only two replicated chromosomes.
words.retrievalPrompt: Count chromosomes, chromatids and homologous pairs in one tetrad.

words.definition: Reciprocal DNA exchange between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during meiotic prophase I.

structure.text: A process phrase; crossover can name one exchange event. It does not mean entire homologues trade places.

words.whatItDoes: Reciprocal exchange between non-sister chromatids creates new linked-allele combinations.
words.commonConfusion: Exchange is not normally between unrelated loci on arbitrary chromosomes.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can crossing over change allele combinations without changing the number of chromosomes?

words.definition: The visible physical connection between homologous chromosomes associated with an earlier crossing-over event.

structure.text: One chiasma, multiple chiasmata. This names a visible connection associated with exchange, not every contact between DNA strands.

words.whatItDoes: The connection marks a crossover-associated link between homologues and helps maintain their association before separation.
words.commonConfusion: A visible chiasma is not the same thing as a centromere.
words.retrievalPrompt: How does a chiasma relate to an earlier DNA exchange?

words.definition: The meiotic stage when homologous chromosome pairs align before their separation.

structure.text: Metaphase names the stage; Roman I identifies the first meiotic division with paired homologues.

words.whatItDoes: Paired homologues align so opposite members can be distributed to different poles.
words.commonConfusion: Homologues align as pairs here; this is not the same arrangement as mitotic metaphase.
words.retrievalPrompt: What arrangement would identify metaphase I rather than mitotic metaphase?

words.definition: The way one homologous pair can align independently of another pair in meiosis I.

structure.text: Orientation names spatial arrangement; independent describes the relationship between different homologous pairs.

words.whatItDoes: The orientation of one homologous pair need not determine the orientation of another pair.
words.commonConfusion: This chromosome-pair independence does not imply all genes on one chromosome assort independently.
words.retrievalPrompt: For two chromosome pairs, explain how alternative orientations produce different parental combinations.

words.definition: The meiotic stage when homologous chromosomes move toward opposite poles while sisters remain associated.

structure.text: Anaphase names separation; Roman I identifies homolog separation in the first meiotic division.

words.whatItDoes: Homologues segregate to opposite poles while sister chromatids normally remain associated.
words.commonConfusion: Normal anaphase I separates homologues, not sister chromatids.
words.retrievalPrompt: Track one maternal homologue and its sister chromatids through anaphase I.

words.definition: A decrease in chromosome-set number from diploid to haploid during the first meiotic division.

structure.text: Reduction is the noun; reductional describes the division that reduces chromosome-set number, not every fall in DNA amount.

words.whatItDoes: Separating homologous sets changes the complement from two sets to one in each resulting meiotic cell.
words.commonConfusion: Reducing set number is not the same as merely reducing DNA amount.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does meiosis I reduce ploidy even though each retained chromosome still has two chromatids?

words.definition: The meiotic division in which sister chromatids separate without another preceding DNA replication.

structure.text: Meiosis names the process; Roman II identifies the division following meiosis I without an intervening DNA-replication phase.

words.whatItDoes: A second spindle division separates sisters from the chromosomes retained after meiosis I.
words.commonConfusion: There is no intervening S phase in the ordinary meiotic sequence.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why would another replication between divisions alter the expected meiotic products?

words.definition: Movement of sister chromatids apart, after which each is counted as a daughter chromosome.

structure.text: Separation names the event; sister specifies chromatids produced by replication rather than homologues.

words.whatItDoes: Loss of sister association allows the two copies to move as independent chromosomes.
words.commonConfusion: After separation, chromosome counts must be updated even though no replication occurs.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain the counting change when four sister chromatids separate into four daughter chromosomes.

words.definition: A cell containing one complete chromosome set after a specified division or life-cycle transition.

structure.text: Product means an output cell; haploid specifies one chromosome set, not necessarily one chromatid per chromosome.

words.whatItDoes: The cell contains one representative set available for its next life-cycle role.
words.commonConfusion: A haploid product is not necessarily an animal gamete; it can be a spore.
words.retrievalPrompt: Compare the next event for a haploid plant spore and a haploid animal gamete.

words.definition: A two-division process following one DNA replication that produces haploid cells and generates genetic variation.

structure.text: Meiosis names the two-division process; meiotic is the adjective. It is distinct from mitosis despite the similar spelling.

words.whatItDoes: One replication followed by two segregations reduces sets and reshuffles inherited combinations.
words.commonConfusion: Meiosis is not two ordinary mitoses with replication before each.
words.retrievalPrompt: Account for the reduction in set number and generation of variation in one meiotic sequence.

words.definition: Differences in DNA sequences or chromosome content among cells or organisms. Mutation can originate variants, and recombination can create new combinations; environment and development also affect phenotypes without necessarily changing inherited DNA.

structure.text: Variation is the head noun; genetic identifies heritable sequence or allele differences rather than every visible difference.

words.whatItDoes: Sequence changes and rearrangements supply differences; recombination redistributes existing variants.
words.commonConfusion: Not every phenotypic difference is an inherited DNA difference.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can siblings differ genetically without requiring a new mutation at every differing locus?

words.definition: Development of sperm through mitosis, meiosis, and cellular differentiation in the testes.

structure.text: Spermato- refers to sperm; -genesis means formation. The term covers sperm production, not only the final shaping stage.

words.whatItDoes: Germ-cell multiplication, meiosis and differentiation produce specialized sperm.
words.commonConfusion: Completing meiosis does not alone produce a fully specialized mature sperm.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish chromosome reduction from the later shaping of a sperm cell.

words.definition: Development of female gametes through mitosis, growth, meiosis, and unequal cytokinesis.

structure.text: Oo- refers to egg and -genesis to formation. The term covers egg-cell development, not only ovulation.

words.whatItDoes: Growth and unequal meiotic divisions retain much of the cytoplasm in the developing egg lineage.
words.commonConfusion: Four meiotic chromosome products do not mean four equivalent functional eggs.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does unequal cytokinesis change cell sizes without changing the need to segregate chromosomes?

words.definition: A small haploid cell produced by unequal cytokinesis during oogenesis that usually does not become an egg.

structure.text: Body names the small cell; polar identifies the conventional name of the asymmetric oogenesis product.

words.whatItDoes: A small cell receives a meiotic chromosome complement while the egg lineage retains most cytoplasm.
words.commonConfusion: A polar body is not simply discarded cytoplasm without chromosomes.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how a polar body can be haploid despite its small size.

words.definition: An interval during which a meiotic process is arrested at a particular stage.

structure.text: Meiotic identifies the process; pause names an arrest in progression, not destruction of the oocyte.

words.whatItDoes: Progression is arrested at a defined meiotic stage until suitable signals permit continuation.
words.commonConfusion: A pause is not automatically completion of meiosis or cell death.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must a description of a paused oocyte name its stage before giving chromosome counts?

words.definition: Independent orientation and separation of different homologous chromosome pairs during meiosis, producing independent allele assortment for unlinked loci.

structure.text: Assortment concerns allocation of alleles; independent states a relationship that does not apply to every pair of loci.

words.whatItDoes: Unlinked loci can distribute independently because different homologous pairs orient independently.
words.commonConfusion: Close linked genes need not produce the independent-assortment ratios.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is a 9:3:3:1 prediction conditional on more than simply having two loci?

words.definition: The combination of gametes without a fixed pairing pattern in the model, adding new allele combinations.

structure.text: Fertilization names gamete union; random specifies an assumption about which gametes unite.

words.whatItDoes: Combining independently produced gametes multiplies possible genotype combinations in the model.
words.commonConfusion: Random pairing is a modelling assumption, not proof that every gamete has equal survival.
words.retrievalPrompt: How do gamete probabilities combine to predict a zygote genotype under random fertilization?

words.definition: A segregation error in the first division, such as homologues failing to separate normally.

structure.text: Error is qualified by the division number: I concerns the first meiotic separation, not automatically any abnormal gamete.

words.whatItDoes: Failure of homologous separation can distribute both homologues to one daughter lineage.
words.commonConfusion: Its typical product pattern differs from one meiosis II nondisjunction event.
words.retrievalPrompt: If one homologous pair fails to separate in meiosis I, how are all four products affected for that chromosome?

words.definition: A segregation error in the second division, such as sister chromatids failing to separate normally.

structure.text: Roman II places the error in the second meiotic division, when sister chromatids should separate.

words.whatItDoes: Failure of sister separation in one daughter cell changes two of the resulting chromosome products.
words.commonConfusion: A second-division error need not affect products from the other first-division daughter.
words.retrievalPrompt: Contrast the four-product pattern from one meiosis II nondisjunction with a meiosis I error.

words.definition: A chromosome number with one or more individual chromosomes added or missing rather than a complete set change.

structure.text: Aneuploid is the adjective; aneuploidy is the condition. It describes individual chromosome imbalance, unlike whole-set polyploidy.

words.whatItDoes: Gain or loss of an individual chromosome changes dosage of genes on that chromosome.
words.commonConfusion: Aneuploidy is not an extra complete chromosome set.
words.retrievalPrompt: For 2n = 6, distinguish a seven-chromosome aneuploid complement from a triploid complement.

words.definition: Twins arising from two separate fertilizations; they are also called dizygotic twins.

structure.text: Twins is the head noun; fraternal is the conventional label for dizygotic twins and does not mean both are male.

words.whatItDoes: Two gametes from each parental contribution form two separate zygotes that develop concurrently.
words.commonConfusion: They are not genetically equivalent to two copies of one zygote.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can fraternal twins differ genetically like other siblings?

words.definition: Twins arising when one early embryo separates into two; they are also called monozygotic twins and need not share every later trait.

structure.text: Identical is the conventional label for monozygotic twins, not a promise of identical environments or every later mutation.

words.whatItDoes: Separation of an early embryonic lineage produces two embryos with very similar initial genomes.
words.commonConfusion: Shared origin does not guarantee identical environments, gene expression or all later traits.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can identical twins develop a phenotypic difference without changing their common origin?

words.definition: A simplified label for separation of one early embryonic lineage into two developing embryos.

structure.text: Zygote identifies the early developmental origin; splitting describes separation into developmental lineages.

words.whatItDoes: One early lineage separates into two embryonic developmental paths.
words.commonConfusion: The simplified label does not mean two sperm fertilized the same egg.
words.retrievalPrompt: How does lineage separation differ from the origin of fraternal twins?

words.definition: A cell or organism descended asexually from one source and therefore highly similar genetically, though not necessarily identical in phenotype.

structure.text: Clone can be noun or verb; clonal is the adjective. Its meaning depends on whether the unit is a molecule, cell or organism.

words.whatItDoes: Asexual descent preserves a closely related genome while later mutations and environments can introduce differences.
words.commonConfusion: Clone does not guarantee identical phenotype or zero subsequent mutation.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can two cloned plants grow differently in different light conditions?

words.definition: Reproduction involving meiosis and fusion of gametes, generating new combinations of genetic information.

structure.text: Reproduction names production of offspring; sexual refers to a gamete-based life cycle, not necessarily two separate parents.

words.whatItDoes: Meiosis and gamete fusion generate combinations from parental genetic contributions.
words.commonConfusion: Two parents are not a sufficient mechanistic definition when life cycles include self-fertilization.
words.retrievalPrompt: Identify the roles of reduction and fusion in maintaining chromosome sets across generations.

words.definition: Reproduction from one parent without gamete fusion, usually producing genetically similar descendants except for mutation.

structure.text: A- negates sexual in this phrase. Asexual reproduction does not include gamete fusion.

words.whatItDoes: A lineage produces offspring without gamete fusion, retaining much of its genetic combination.
words.commonConfusion: Asexual descendants can still acquire mutations.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can an asexual population contain genetic differences over many generations?

words.definition: A multicellular haploid stage that produces gametes by mitosis in a plant life cycle.

structure.text: Gamete plus -phyte, plant: the plant generation that produces gametes. Its name identifies its product.

words.whatItDoes: The haploid multicellular stage produces gametes through mitotic divisions.
words.commonConfusion: A haploid gametophyte does not normally halve its set again to produce gametes.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can a gametophyte make haploid gametes by mitosis?

words.definition: A multicellular diploid stage that produces haploid spores through meiosis in a plant life cycle.

structure.text: Spore plus -phyte, plant: the plant generation that produces spores. It does not mean a single spore.

words.whatItDoes: The diploid multicellular stage makes haploid spores by meiosis.
words.commonConfusion: Spores from the sporophyte are not already equivalent to its gametes.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace the chromosome-set change when a sporophyte produces spores.

words.definition: In the plant life cycles studied here, a haploid reproductive cell that grows by cell division into the haploid stage without first joining another reproductive cell.

structure.text: Spore is the noun; spores is plural. In a plant life cycle it differs from a gamete by not needing fusion to begin development.

words.whatItDoes: A plant spore grows into a haploid stage by division without requiring fusion first.
words.commonConfusion: A spore is not a gamete simply because both are haploid.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which next event distinguishes a spore from a gamete in the plant cycle studied?

words.definition: A haploid reproductive cell—sperm or egg lineage cell—that can contribute one chromosome set at fertilization.

structure.text: Gamete names a reproductive cell; gametic is the adjective. It is not the same as gonad, a reproductive organ.

words.whatItDoes: At fertilization its chromosome set combines with another gamete's set.
words.commonConfusion: Haploid cells are not all gametes.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how two haploid gametes restore a diploid complement.

words.definition: A genus of small aquatic crustaceans used here to compare environmentally influenced sexual and asexual reproductive strategies.

structure.text: A capitalized genus name, conventionally italicized. It names organisms, not a reproductive mechanism.

words.whatItDoes: These animals illustrate reproductive strategies that can shift with environmental conditions and life-cycle stage.
words.commonConfusion: A named example does not mean all Daphnia always reproduce in the same mode.
words.retrievalPrompt: What evidence would establish whether a particular Daphnia brood arose sexually or asexually?

words.definition: An animal used here to compare sexual reproduction with asexual processes such as budding or fission.

structure.text: A common organism name; sea distinguishes the animal from the flowering plant called anemone.

words.whatItDoes: Its reproductive examples show that one animal lineage can use sexual reproduction and certain asexual processes.
words.commonConfusion: Not every cnidarian has the same alternation of body forms.
words.retrievalPrompt: What observation distinguishes an anemone produced by fission from one developing after fertilization?

words.definition: A usually attached body form of some cnidarians; its life-cycle role depends on the species.

structure.text: A body-form noun; polyp stage identifies an attached cnidarian form, not a particular sex.

words.whatItDoes: The attached body form can feed and participate in species-specific reproductive stages.
words.commonConfusion: Polyp does not universally mean diploid asexual generation in a plant-like alternation.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must the species be specified before assigning a polyp's reproductive role?

words.definition: A usually free-swimming body form of some cnidarians; not all cnidarians have this stage.

structure.text: One medusa, multiple medusae. The name describes a cnidarian body form rather than an allele or life-cycle ploidy.

words.whatItDoes: A free-swimming cnidarian body form participates in the life cycle of species that have it.
words.commonConfusion: Not all cnidarians produce medusae.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why would adding a medusa stage to every cnidarian diagram be incorrect?

words.definition: Producing genetically closely related cells or organisms from a source lineage; environmental and later genetic differences can remain.

structure.text: The -ing form names a process of producing copies; specify gene, cell or organism cloning.

words.whatItDoes: A source lineage is reproduced with high genetic similarity, while development remains environment-dependent.
words.commonConfusion: Cloning an organism is not copying all its experiences or acquired characteristics.
words.retrievalPrompt: Separate genetic similarity from phenotypic identity in a cloning claim.

words.definition: A favourable outcome for a specified person, group or system, evaluated using stated criteria.

structure.text: A noun for a favourable consequence relative to a stated goal. Beneficial does not mean risk-free.

words.whatItDoes: A stated criterion makes a favourable consequence evaluable for a particular stakeholder.
words.commonConfusion: A benefit to one group does not establish a benefit to everyone.
words.retrievalPrompt: Name a potential benefit of cloning a crop and specify who benefits and how it would be measured.

words.definition: A boundary on what a method, dataset or model can establish.

structure.text: A noun derived from limit; it identifies a boundary on what a method or result can establish.

words.whatItDoes: A stated boundary prevents a finding from being applied beyond its evidence or assumptions.
words.commonConfusion: A limitation does not automatically make a method worthless.
words.retrievalPrompt: What limitation should accompany a reproduction simulation that excludes mutation?

words.definition: Presenting a question, method, evidence and explanation clearly enough for another reader to assess them.

structure.text: A process noun for conveying meaning. Scientific communication includes conditions and uncertainty, not only a result.

words.whatItDoes: Clear method, evidence and reasoning allow others to assess and reproduce an argument.
words.commonConfusion: An attractive diagram cannot replace a missing explanation of its symbols.
words.retrievalPrompt: What information must accompany a chromosome diagram so another reader can check its counts?

words.definition: One of two or more DNA-sequence versions at a gene or locus.

structure.text: Allele is the noun; allelic is the adjective. Different alleles occupy the same locus on corresponding chromosomes.

words.whatItDoes: Different sequence versions can yield different gene products or expression patterns.
words.commonConfusion: An allele is not a separate gene position.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how two alleles can occupy the same locus on homologous chromosomes.

words.definition: The allele combination an organism or cell carries at one or more loci.

structure.text: Geno- relates to genetic constitution; type identifies the allele combination, not the observable phenotype.

words.whatItDoes: The specified allele combination defines the genetic starting information for an inheritance prediction.
words.commonConfusion: A phenotype need not uniquely reveal a genotype.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can two dominant-phenotype individuals have different genotypes?

words.definition: An observable or measurable characteristic produced through genotype, gene expression, development, and environment.

structure.text: Phenotype is the observable-characteristic term; phenotypic is the adjective. It does not encode the cause of that characteristic.

words.whatItDoes: Gene expression, development and environment produce the measured trait.
words.commonConfusion: Phenotype is not determined solely by the allele symbols written in a Punnett square.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could two organisms with the same tested genotype differ in a measured trait?

words.definition: Having two copies of the same allele at a locus in a diploid cell or organism.

structure.text: Homo- means same; the complete adjective describes matching alleles at the specified locus.

words.whatItDoes: Matching allele copies constrain the allele type contributed at that locus in the simple segregation model.
words.commonConfusion: Homozygous does not automatically mean dominant or healthy.
words.retrievalPrompt: Compare the gametes possible from AA and aa at one locus.

words.definition: Having two different alleles at a locus in a diploid cell or organism.

structure.text: Hetero- means different; the adjective describes two different alleles at the specified locus.

words.whatItDoes: Two different alleles segregate into different gametes at a simple diploid locus.
words.commonConfusion: Heterozygous does not mean an intermediate phenotype in every inheritance pattern.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can Aa produce two allele types while showing only one scored phenotype?

words.definition: Describes an allele whose scored phenotype appears in a heterozygote under specified conditions.

structure.text: An adjective describing expression in a specified heterozygote. Dominant does not mean common, stronger or healthier.

words.whatItDoes: In a specified heterozygote, the allele's scored trait appears under the stated conditions.
words.commonConfusion: Dominant does not mean common, stronger, beneficial or destined to increase.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does dominance alone not predict an allele's population frequency?

words.definition: Describes an allele whose scored phenotype in simple dominance is usually observed only without a dominant allele.

structure.text: An adjective describing an allele-associated effect masked in a specified heterozygote, not a disappearing allele.

words.whatItDoes: Its simple-dominance phenotype becomes apparent when no dominant allele masks that scored effect.
words.commonConfusion: A recessive allele can still be inherited and expressed molecularly in a heterozygote.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can two parents lacking a recessive phenotype produce a child showing it?

words.definition: An RNA or protein output associated with a gene variant, contributing to how a genotype affects a trait.

structure.text: Product is what expression produces; allele specifies which sequence version is being considered.

words.whatItDoes: RNA or protein differences can connect DNA variation to cellular function and phenotype.
words.commonConfusion: An allele symbol does not itself explain the biochemical mechanism.
words.retrievalPrompt: What additional molecular evidence would connect an allele difference to an enzyme-activity phenotype?

words.definition: A trait influenced by variation at many genetic loci, commonly also affected by environment.

structure.text: Poly- means many; genic concerns genes. Trait is the characteristic influenced by multiple genes.

words.whatItDoes: Variation at several loci combines with development and environment to influence the measured trait.
words.commonConfusion: Many contributing loci do not imply a simple dominant–recessive ratio for the whole trait.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why would a single-locus Punnett square poorly predict variation in a polygenic measurement?

words.definition: An effect of surrounding conditions on development, expression or performance of an organism.

structure.text: Influence is the contribution; environmental identifies conditions rather than an allele sequence.

words.whatItDoes: Conditions can modify expression or development without necessarily changing inherited DNA sequence.
words.commonConfusion: A changed phenotype is not proof of a changed inherited allele.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could a controlled light treatment test an environmental contribution to plant height?

words.definition: A range of measured trait values, often influenced by several genes and environmental conditions.

structure.text: Continuous qualifies the observed distribution: intermediate values occur rather than only separate classes.

words.whatItDoes: Contributing effects produce a range of values rather than only a few discrete classes.
words.commonConfusion: A continuous distribution does not demonstrate that genes have no role.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can many discrete allele combinations contribute to a continuous range of heights?

words.definition: The parental generation in a defined genetic cross.

structure.text: P identifies the parental generation in a cross; it is not an allele symbol or a probability here.

words.whatItDoes: It defines the parental starting cross from which later generations are labelled.
words.commonConfusion: P is relative to the stated experiment, not the oldest ancestors that ever existed.
words.retrievalPrompt: Identify P when two selected lines begin a new cross.

words.definition: The first offspring generation produced by the specified parental cross.

structure.text: F stands for filial; 1 identifies the first offspring generation from the stated parental cross.

words.whatItDoes: It identifies the immediate offspring of the specified P cross.
words.commonConfusion: F1 does not by itself imply heterozygosity at every locus.
words.retrievalPrompt: What must be known about the parents before concluding all F1 offspring are Aa?

words.definition: The second offspring generation, often produced by crossing F1 individuals in the stated model.

structure.text: F stands for filial; 2 identifies the next filial generation, often from crossing F1 individuals.

words.whatItDoes: It identifies offspring from the specified next cross involving F1 individuals.
words.commonConfusion: A familiar F2 ratio requires a stated F1 genotype and inheritance model.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is a 3:1 phenotype prediction not automatic for every F2 generation?

words.definition: Producing the same specified trait when self-fertilized or crossed within the line under the simple model; the relevant loci are homozygous.

structure.text: A breeding-description phrase: the specified trait remains consistent under the stated breeding conditions.

words.whatItDoes: Relevant homozygous loci can produce consistent specified offspring traits in the simple model.
words.commonConfusion: True breeding for one trait does not establish genetic identity across the genome.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can a line breed true for seed colour while varying at other loci?

words.definition: A comparison that switches which parental sex carries each trait or genotype.

structure.text: Cross names the mating comparison; reciprocal reverses which parent supplies each phenotype or genotype.

words.whatItDoes: Switching parental sex roles tests whether transmission depends on which parent carries the allele.
words.commonConfusion: Matching reciprocal outcomes do not alone prove every possible autosomal model.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why might reciprocal crosses differ for an X-linked trait?

words.definition: The two allele copies at a locus in a diploid individual, one associated with each homologue.

structure.text: Pair means two; allele identifies the versions at one locus, not two different genes.

words.whatItDoes: The two homologous copies supply one allele per normal gamete after segregation.
words.commonConfusion: Two copies at a locus are not two different loci.
words.retrievalPrompt: What gamete allele alternatives follow from the pair Aa?

words.definition: Separation of chromosomes or chromatids during cell division. In Mendelian inheritance, allele segregation describes separation of allele-bearing homologues so each normal gamete receives one allele copy at a locus.

structure.text: Segregation names separation; segregate is the verb. Genetic segregation concerns allele distribution into gametes.

words.whatItDoes: Separation of allele-bearing homologues normally leaves one allele copy per gamete at a diploid locus.
words.commonConfusion: Alleles do not blend into one permanent intermediate allele.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how segregation lets a recessive allele reappear after an F1 generation.

words.definition: A model in which a trait-associated allele on an autosome is expressed in the heterozygote.

structure.text: Autosomal locates the locus outside sex chromosomes; dominant describes expression in a heterozygote.

words.whatItDoes: One trait-associated copy can produce the scored phenotype in the stated heterozygote.
words.commonConfusion: An affected person need not be homozygous, and a pedigree pattern is not a diagnosis.
words.retrievalPrompt: For Aa × aa under this model, predict the phenotype probabilities.

words.definition: A model in which two copies of a trait-associated autosomal allele are required for the specified phenotype.

structure.text: Autosomal describes locus location; recessive describes the specified allele effect in heterozygotes.

words.whatItDoes: The specified phenotype occurs when both homologous copies carry the relevant recessive allele in the simple model.
words.commonConfusion: Unaffected parents can be carriers.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can Aa × Aa produce an affected offspring even when both parents are unaffected?

words.definition: A grid that organizes possible gamete combinations to calculate offspring genotype probabilities under stated assumptions.

structure.text: Punnett is a personal name; square describes the organizing grid, not a rule guaranteeing an offspring ratio.

words.whatItDoes: Combining gamete categories organizes genotype probabilities with the appropriate gamete weights.
words.commonConfusion: Equal-sized grid cells are not automatically equally probable when gamete frequencies differ.
words.retrievalPrompt: How would you adapt a Punnett calculation if one parent's gamete types were not equally frequent?

words.definition: A cross with a homozygous recessive partner used to infer an unknown genotype or gamete frequencies.

structure.text: Test modifies cross: the mating is chosen to reveal genotype information rather than merely produce offspring.

words.whatItDoes: A recessive partner makes offspring classes informative about the tested parent's gametes.
words.commonConfusion: A small sample without recessive offspring does not prove the unknown parent is homozygous.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does Aa × aa reveal a different expected pattern from AA × aa?

words.definition: An event whose occurrence does not change the probability of another event under the stated model.

structure.text: Event names an outcome occurrence; independent means its probability is unchanged by the other specified event.

words.whatItDoes: Independence permits multiplication without changing one event's probability after observing the other.
words.commonConfusion: Independent does not mean mutually exclusive.
words.retrievalPrompt: Contrast two independent coin outcomes with two mutually exclusive genotypes of one offspring.

words.definition: Chance variation among finite samples drawn under the same probability model.

structure.text: Fluctuation is variation between observations; sample specifies the finite subset rather than a change in the underlying model.

words.whatItDoes: Finite draws vary around model expectations even when the model remains unchanged.
words.commonConfusion: Observed ratios need not exactly equal expected ratios.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can eight offspring from a 1:1 model divide 5:3 without disproving the model?

words.definition: The probability that a gamete carries a specified allele combination under a stated genetic model.

structure.text: Probability is the chance; gamete specifies the gamete type being counted, not an offspring genotype.

words.whatItDoes: It weights possible allele combinations before combining parental contributions.
words.commonConfusion: Listing four gamete names does not establish equal probabilities under linkage.
words.retrievalPrompt: How would linkage change the weights assigned to AB, Ab, aB and ab?

words.definition: The relative numbers or probabilities of specified genotype classes, written in a stated order; for example, AA:Aa:aa = 1:2:1.

structure.text: Ratio compares genotype counts or expected frequencies; it is not automatically the phenotype ratio.

words.whatItDoes: It compares allele-combination categories in a specified order.
words.commonConfusion: A 1:2:1 genotype ratio need not also be the phenotype ratio.
words.retrievalPrompt: Translate AA:Aa:aa = 1:2:1 into phenotypes under complete dominance.

words.definition: The relative numbers or probabilities of specified observable trait classes, written in a stated order; for example, dominant:recessive = 3:1 in a simple complete-dominance cross.

structure.text: Ratio compares observable classes; phenotype distinguishes those classes from allele combinations.

words.whatItDoes: It groups genotype outcomes according to the scored trait model.
words.commonConfusion: Changing dominance assumptions can change the phenotype ratio without changing the genotype probabilities.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can the same cross give 3:1 under complete dominance but 1:2:1 under incomplete dominance?

words.definition: A probability rule that multiplies probabilities along a sequence of independent or conditional events.

structure.text: Product means multiplication. The probability rule requires independence or the appropriate conditional factors.

words.whatItDoes: Multiplication combines probabilities along a path, using conditional factors where needed.
words.commonConfusion: Independence must not be assumed when one event changes another's probability.
words.retrievalPrompt: Write the probability of A and B using P(A) and P(B given A), then state when it simplifies.

words.definition: A probability rule for mutually exclusive alternatives: add the probabilities of the separate outcomes.

structure.text: Sum means addition. Direct addition applies to mutually exclusive alternatives; overlaps require correction.

words.whatItDoes: Adding probabilities combines mutually exclusive routes to a specified result.
words.commonConfusion: Overlapping outcomes would be double-counted without correcting the overlap.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can the two parental routes to Aa be added in an Aa × Aa cross?

words.definition: Events whose probabilities are unchanged by the outcomes of earlier trials under the model.

structure.text: Trials are repeated opportunities; independent means earlier outcomes do not change the next trial's probabilities.

words.whatItDoes: Earlier trial outcomes do not alter the next trial's probability under the model.
words.commonConfusion: A previous run of one outcome does not make the opposite outcome due.
words.retrievalPrompt: After three recessive offspring, what is the next-offspring risk in the same Aa × Aa model?

words.definition: The four allele combinations AB, Ab, aB and ab available from AaBb when the two loci assort independently.

structure.text: Four is a count of possible classes, not four cells or an automatic guarantee of equal frequencies.

words.whatItDoes: Unlinked AaBb can contribute AB, Ab, aB and ab, each with probability one quarter under equal segregation.
words.commonConfusion: The list does not remain equally weighted for linked loci.
words.retrievalPrompt: Derive the probability of Ab from the separate A and b probabilities.

words.definition: Two positions on chromosomes being followed in a genetic model; linkage must be specified.

structure.text: Loci is the plural of locus; two loci means two positions, not two alleles at one position.

words.whatItDoes: Following two positions requires specifying allele combinations and whether the positions are linked.
words.commonConfusion: Two loci do not mean two alleles at one locus.
words.retrievalPrompt: What extra information is needed beyond AaBb to predict linked gamete frequencies?

words.definition: The number actually measured in a category before comparison with a model.

structure.text: Count is a number of cases; observed distinguishes recorded data from a model prediction.

words.whatItDoes: It records measured category membership before model comparison.
words.commonConfusion: An observed count should not be replaced by a rounded theoretical ratio.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must the original counts be retained when comparing a small cross with an expected ratio?

words.definition: The number predicted for a category by a specified probability model and total sample size.

structure.text: Expected distinguishes a model-derived count from what must happen in a particular sample.

words.whatItDoes: Multiplying total sample size by model probability gives the predicted category count.
words.commonConfusion: An expectation can be fractional even though observed individuals are whole numbers.
words.retrievalPrompt: For 30 offspring and probability one quarter, calculate the expected count and explain the fraction.

words.definition: The number of observations or individuals included in the sample.

structure.text: Size is the number of sampled units. State whether the units are offspring, gametes, people or allele copies.

words.whatItDoes: It sets the amount of information and the scale of expected counts.
words.commonConfusion: A large sample reduces chance fluctuation but does not remove systematic bias.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why are conclusions from four offspring less stable than from 400 under the same model?

words.definition: A heterozygote with a phenotype between the two homozygous phenotypes under incomplete dominance.

structure.text: Heterozygote specifies allele combination; intermediate describes its phenotype under incomplete dominance.

words.whatItDoes: Incomplete dominance gives a scored heterozygote phenotype between the two homozygotes.
words.commonConfusion: Intermediate appearance does not mean alleles permanently blend.
words.retrievalPrompt: What F2 genotype and phenotype ratios follow when both homozygotes and the heterozygote are distinguishable?

words.definition: An inheritance pattern in which both alleles in a heterozygote contribute distinct detectable products or traits.

structure.text: Co- means together; dominance concerns expression. Both allele-associated products are detectable in the heterozygote.

words.whatItDoes: Both allelic contributions remain detectably distinct in the heterozygote.
words.commonConfusion: Codominance is not necessarily an averaged intermediate trait.
words.retrievalPrompt: Contrast detecting both A and B antigens with an intermediate phenotype.

words.definition: A human blood-group system controlled by multiple alleles in which IA and IB are codominant and i is recessive.

structure.text: A, B and O label blood-group categories; the letters are not a word to split into roots.

words.whatItDoes: Allele combinations determine the standard A, B, AB and O antigen-pattern categories.
words.commonConfusion: Three population alleles do not mean one diploid individual carries three copies at this locus.
words.retrievalPrompt: What offspring ABO phenotypes are possible from IAi × IBi?

words.definition: Three or more allele versions present at one locus in a population, though a diploid individual carries at most two.

structure.text: Multiple describes more than two alternatives in a population, not necessarily more than two copies in one diploid individual.

words.whatItDoes: A population can contain several sequence alternatives while each diploid individual carries two copies.
words.commonConfusion: Population allele diversity is not an individual's ploidy.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can a three-allele locus still produce an individual with only two alleles?

words.definition: Describes a gene located on the X chromosome and its associated inheritance pattern.

structure.text: X names the chromosome; linked locates the locus there. It does not mean only males can carry the allele.

words.whatItDoes: Transmission follows the X chromosome contributions specified for the cross.
words.commonConfusion: An XY father does not normally pass his X chromosome to an XY son.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace a father's X-linked allele to possible offspring in the standard XX/XY model.

words.definition: Describes a gene located on the Y chromosome and transmitted through Y-bearing lineages.

structure.text: Y names the chromosome; linked specifies locus location, not a generic male-associated characteristic.

words.whatItDoes: A locus in the Y-specific region follows Y-bearing transmission in the stated model.
words.commonConfusion: A trait expressed only in males is not automatically Y-linked.
words.retrievalPrompt: What pedigree transmission would be consistent with a Y-specific allele under the standard model?

words.definition: Located on, or inherited through, an autosome.

structure.text: The adjective formed from autosome; it identifies chromosome location rather than dominance.

words.whatItDoes: The locus follows an autosome rather than the sex-chromosome transmission pattern.
words.commonConfusion: Autosomal does not mean dominant.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must both chromosome location and dominance pattern be specified?

words.definition: Having only one copy of a gene or chromosome region in a diploid cell, as for many X-linked loci in XY cells.

structure.text: Hemi- means half; in this context the individual has one copy at the specified locus instead of a diploid pair.

words.whatItDoes: A single allele copy can be expressed without a corresponding second copy at that region.
words.commonConfusion: Hemizygous is not the same as homozygous.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is an XY individual commonly hemizygous for an X-specific locus?

words.definition: A trait influenced by variation at many genetic loci, commonly also affected by environment.

structure.text: Poly- means many; -genic concerns genes. The adjective describes multi-gene influence.

words.whatItDoes: Contributions from several loci influence one measured trait.
words.commonConfusion: Polygenic inheritance differs from multiple alleles at a single locus.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish a many-locus trait from a three-allele blood-group locus.

words.definition: The physical, biological and other surrounding conditions relevant to an organism or process.

structure.text: Environment is the conditions noun; environmental is the adjective. It includes more than outdoor habitat.

words.whatItDoes: Surrounding conditions can influence development, expression and the measurements obtained.
words.commonConfusion: Environment is not limited to climate and does not exclude biological interactions.
words.retrievalPrompt: Name a biological and a physical environmental variable that could affect a phenotype.

words.definition: A stated set of rules linking parental alleles, gametes and offspring genotypes/phenotypes.

structure.text: Model is the explanation framework; inheritance specifies how allele transmission and expression are represented.

words.whatItDoes: Explicit rules turn parental information into testable offspring predictions.
words.commonConfusion: A model fitting a small pedigree need not be the only explanation.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which assumptions must be stated before predicting a recessive-trait probability?

words.definition: The symbols and conventions used to represent biological quantities or relationships.

structure.text: Notation names a symbol system. A consistent key determines what capitals, subscripts and superscripts mean.

words.whatItDoes: Consistent symbols keep loci, allele relationships and chromosome phase interpretable.
words.commonConfusion: Capital letters are conventions, not evidence that an allele is common.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must a problem define whether AB/ab indicates linkage phase rather than two independent symbols?

words.definition: The probability of an event after specified information or a condition is taken into account.

structure.text: Conditional modifies probability: the denominator is restricted to cases satisfying the stated condition.

words.whatItDoes: Restricting the sample space to known information changes the appropriate denominator.
words.commonConfusion: An unconditional one-quarter risk cannot be reused after excluding affected offspring.
words.retrievalPrompt: Among unaffected offspring of Aa × Aa, what fraction are carriers?

words.definition: A diagram of reported trait occurrence and relationships across generations, interpreted probabilistically and with privacy safeguards.

structure.text: Pedigree is a family-relationship record; pedigree analysis is the inference process using that record.

words.whatItDoes: Family relationships and reported phenotypes constrain, but may not uniquely determine, inheritance models.
words.commonConfusion: A pedigree is not proof of genotype or permission to disclose a person's data.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can two different inheritance models fit a small pedigree?

words.definition: A group or stage in a parent-to-offspring sequence, defined for the population being studied.

structure.text: A generational level in a pedigree differs from one particular individual or a fixed number of years.

words.whatItDoes: It locates individuals within a stated parent-to-offspring sequence.
words.commonConfusion: Generation labels are contextual rather than a direct measure of elapsed years.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can two species complete different numbers of generations in the same time?

words.definition: One organism or labelled case in the stated population or pedigree.

structure.text: A noun naming one organism in the pedigree, not one allele or one mating pair.

words.whatItDoes: A labelled organism provides a case whose observed phenotype and inferred genotype must be distinguished.
words.commonConfusion: One individual is not a representative population frequency.
words.retrievalPrompt: Separate what is observed and what is inferred for an untested pedigree individual.

words.definition: A pedigree label indicating the specified phenotype; it is not a judgment about the person.

structure.text: An adjective marking the recorded phenotype. It does not, on its own, name the genotype.

words.whatItDoes: It marks presence of the phenotype defined for the pedigree analysis.
words.commonConfusion: The label does not describe a person's worth or establish every aspect of health.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must the scored phenotype be defined before marking individuals as affected?

words.definition: A pedigree label indicating absence of the specified phenotype; it does not necessarily establish genotype.

structure.text: Un- negates affected for the recorded phenotype; it does not rule out carrier status.

words.whatItDoes: It records absence of the specified phenotype at the stated observation.
words.commonConfusion: Unaffected does not guarantee absence of a recessive allele.
words.retrievalPrompt: Under a recessive model, which genotypes can be unaffected?

words.definition: In simple recessive inheritance, a heterozygous individual who has one recessive allele and usually lacks the associated phenotype.

structure.text: A person-level label tied to a specified recessive condition; carriage is not evidence of the affected phenotype.

words.whatItDoes: A heterozygote can transmit the recessive allele despite lacking its simple-model phenotype.
words.commonConfusion: Carrier is specific to the inheritance model, not a synonym for every person with an allele.
words.retrievalPrompt: What gametes can an unaffected carrier produce at the specified locus?

words.definition: An allele combination not uniquely determined by the available evidence.

structure.text: Unknown describes missing information, not an additional allele or biological genotype class.

words.whatItDoes: Evidence leaves more than one allele combination possible.
words.commonConfusion: An untested genotype should not be replaced by the most convenient certainty.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must an unaffected child of two carriers remain AA or Aa rather than automatically Aa?

words.definition: Describes a gene located on the X chromosome and its associated inheritance pattern.

structure.text: Inheritance is the transmission pattern; X-linked identifies the chromosomal location involved.

words.whatItDoes: An X-specific locus follows different possible transmissions depending on parental chromosome contributions.
words.commonConfusion: Father-to-son transmission in the standard model does not support an X-specific route.
words.retrievalPrompt: How does the father's contribution differ for an XX offspring and an XY offspring?

words.definition: Passage of genetic information from a parent through a gamete to offspring.

structure.text: Transmission is the passing-on process; transmitted is the participle. It need not mean phenotype expression.

words.whatItDoes: A gamete carries genetic information into the next generation.
words.commonConfusion: Transmission of an allele does not guarantee the same phenotype in offspring.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can a parent pass an allele without the offspring showing the parent's scored phenotype?

words.definition: A different explanation that can be compared against the same observations.

structure.text: Alternative marks a competing explanation; model identifies assumptions to compare against evidence.

words.whatItDoes: Competing explanations can be tested against the same observations and new discriminating evidence.
words.commonConfusion: Failure to reject one model does not eliminate all alternatives.
words.retrievalPrompt: What additional family observation could distinguish two models that fit the current pedigree?

words.definition: A numerical measure of how likely an event is under a stated model, from zero to one.

structure.text: Probability is a numerical chance between zero and one, not a guaranteed fraction in a small family.

words.whatItDoes: It quantifies a model's likelihood for an outcome rather than promising a particular small-sample result.
words.commonConfusion: A probability of one quarter does not mean exactly one in every four siblings.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain the difference between a predicted probability and an observed family outcome.

words.definition: Control and appropriate protection of personal information, including genetic information.

structure.text: Privacy concerns control of personal information; private genetic information is not automatically shared family consent.

words.whatItDoes: Appropriate limits on access and disclosure protect genetic information and its wider family implications.
words.commonConfusion: Removing a name does not always make a detailed pedigree unidentifiable.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can sharing one person's genetic result also reveal information about relatives?

words.definition: An informed and voluntary agreement to a specified use or procedure; one agreement does not authorize every later use.

structure.text: Consent names informed permission for a particular use, not merely possession of a genetic sample.

words.whatItDoes: A specific informed agreement defines the authorized use of information or a procedure.
words.commonConfusion: Agreement to one study does not authorize every future use.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why should permission for a classroom pedigree example be separate from public posting?

words.definition: Gene positions on the same chromosome; nearby positions tend to be inherited together because crossing over separates them less often.

structure.text: Loci is plural of locus; linked specifies positions on the same chromosome considered in inheritance.

words.whatItDoes: Nearby loci on one chromosome tend to retain their parental association because fewer crossovers separate them.
words.commonConfusion: Being on the same chromosome does not guarantee an observed recombinant fraction below 50% for distant loci.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why do nearby loci generally produce more parental than recombinant combinations?

words.definition: Coming from a parent or original generation. In a linkage cross, parental combinations match allele arrangements present on the original parental chromosomes; distinguish that narrower use from recombinant combinations.

structure.text: An adjective for allele combinations matching the original parental arrangement, not only the parent organisms themselves.

words.whatItDoes: In linkage analysis it identifies the original allele arrangements used as the comparison baseline.
words.commonConfusion: Parental phenotype and parental chromosome phase are different descriptions.
words.retrievalPrompt: For AB/ab, identify the parental gamete classes before classifying recombinants.

words.definition: An offspring or gamete allele combination different from the parental chromosome arrangements.

structure.text: Re- suggests recombination; recombinant labels a new combination relative to the parental arrangement.

words.whatItDoes: Rearranged allele combinations differ from the original chromosome phase in the stated cross.
words.commonConfusion: A rare class is not automatically recombinant without knowing parental phase.
words.retrievalPrompt: For Ab/aB, which gamete combinations are recombinant?

words.definition: The number of offspring classified as nonparental combinations in the stated cross.

structure.text: Count is the number classified as recombinant; it is the numerator, not the recombination percentage.

words.whatItDoes: It totals all classes classified as recombinant using the cross's phase.
words.commonConfusion: Counting only one reciprocal recombinant class underestimates the total.
words.retrievalPrompt: Given AB = 40, ab = 40, Ab = 10 and aB = 10 from AB/ab, find the recombinant count.

words.definition: All offspring included in the comparison, including parental and recombinant classes.

structure.text: Total sets the denominator across all scored offspring, including both parental and recombinant classes.

words.whatItDoes: It supplies the denominator including both parental and recombinant classes.
words.commonConfusion: The denominator is not just the sum of the rare classes.
words.retrievalPrompt: Using 20 recombinants among 100 offspring, identify both numerator and denominator of recombination frequency.

words.definition: A linkage-map distance equal to a one-percent recombination frequency; also called a centimorgan.

structure.text: Unit names a scale increment on a genetic map, not a fixed number of DNA bases.

words.whatItDoes: One percent recombination gives an approximate short-interval linkage distance.
words.commonConfusion: A centimorgan is not a fixed physical number of DNA bases.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can equal map distances correspond to different physical lengths in different regions?

words.definition: An estimated separation between two gene loci, expressed in a stated mapping unit.

structure.text: Pairwise specifies a two-locus comparison; distance is an inferred genetic interval, not physical centimetres.

words.whatItDoes: Comparing two loci estimates their linkage separation from recombinant frequency or other mapping evidence.
words.commonConfusion: Adding long pairwise recombination percentages can obscure multiple crossovers.
words.retrievalPrompt: What assumption supports treating a small recombinant percentage as a map distance?

words.definition: The relative arrangement of loci along a chromosome inferred from recombination evidence or physical mapping.

structure.text: Order is the sequence of loci along a chromosome; it is distinct from the alphabetical order of gene labels.
