words.whatItDoes: Relative distances and recombination patterns constrain which locus lies between the others.
words.commonConfusion: One pairwise distance cannot determine the order of three loci.
words.retrievalPrompt: If AB = 5, BC = 8 and AC = 13 map units, propose an order and its reverse.

words.definition: A map drawn in the opposite left-to-right direction while preserving the same gene order relationships and distances.

structure.text: Reversed changes drawing orientation; the same locus order and interval relationships can be represented from either end.

words.whatItDoes: Reversing the drawing preserves biological adjacency and distances.
words.commonConfusion: Left-to-right orientation is not an additional biological inference without a reference.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why do A–B–C and C–B–A express the same relative order?

words.definition: The maximum expected recombinant fraction between two loci under the standard mapping model; larger map distances may be obscured by multiple crossovers.

structure.text: Ceiling means an upper observable limit; fifty percent is a recombination-frequency boundary, not a maximum physical separation.

words.whatItDoes: Multiple exchanges can make distant linked loci behave like unlinked loci in a two-point cross.
words.commonConfusion: A measured 50% does not prove two loci are on different chromosomes.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can a chromosome map exceed 50 map units while a two-point recombinant fraction approaches 50%?

words.definition: Two or more crossing-over events within the chromosome interval being studied.

structure.text: Multiple describes more than one exchange; crossover names an exchange event within the interval considered.

words.whatItDoes: Two or more exchanges can restore parental arrangements at outside markers while altering internal intervals.
words.commonConfusion: Outside-marker scoring can miss an even number of exchanges.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how a double crossover may escape a two-marker recombinant count.

words.definition: Chance difference between a sample result and the underlying probabilities or population because only a finite sample was observed.

structure.text: Uncertainty is the imprecision; sampling identifies variation arising from the finite observed subset.

words.whatItDoes: Finite observations make measured recombinant frequencies fluctuate around model probabilities.
words.commonConfusion: A sample percentage is not an exact physical constant.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why should a distance estimated from 20 offspring be interpreted more cautiously than one from 2,000?

words.definition: Uptake and expression of external genetic material by a cell; in biotechnology it often introduces a plasmid into bacteria.

structure.text: Transformation is the process noun; transformed describes a cell changed through uptake of external genetic material here.

words.whatItDoes: A cell takes up external genetic material that can produce a heritable or expressed change under suitable conditions.
words.commonConfusion: Transformation is not bacterial reproduction or necessarily transfer of an entire chromosome.
words.retrievalPrompt: What control distinguishes an effect of introduced DNA from an effect of the treatment itself?

words.definition: A comparison or controlled condition that helps isolate an interpretation of an experimental result.

structure.text: Control is a comparison condition; experimental distinguishes it from biological regulation or a control centre.

words.whatItDoes: A comparison isolates plausible causes of a measured difference.
words.commonConfusion: A control group does not eliminate every confounding variable automatically.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why compare a DNA-treated bacterial sample with a similarly treated sample lacking the DNA?

words.definition: A molecule made of a chain or chains of small building blocks called amino acids; its sequence and folded shape help determine its function.

structure.text: Protein is the molecule-class noun; protein-coding describes a sequence whose expression specifies a polypeptide.

words.whatItDoes: Amino-acid sequence and folding create structures that catalyze, transport, signal or provide support.
words.commonConfusion: A protein is not a nucleic-acid chain.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could changing an amino acid affect protein function without changing protein length?

words.definition: A chemical group in the nucleic-acid backbone that contributes to its negative charge and connections between sugars.

structure.text: Phosphate names the chemical group; it is not interchangeable with phosphorus, the element.

words.whatItDoes: Phosphate links sugars in the backbone and contributes negative charge.
words.commonConfusion: Phosphate groups are not the variable bases encoding the sequence.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which DNA component helps explain movement toward the positive electrode in a gel?

words.definition: The five-carbon sugar found in DNA nucleotides.

structure.text: Deoxy- distinguishes the sugar from ribose by an oxygen difference. The name does not mean the sugar contains no oxygen.

words.whatItDoes: The DNA sugar connects a base to the sugar–phosphate backbone and establishes strand direction.
words.commonConfusion: Deoxyribose is not a nitrogenous base.
words.retrievalPrompt: Where does the sugar fit relative to the base and phosphate in a DNA nucleotide?

words.definition: One of the information-bearing chemical units in DNA or RNA; ordinary DNA uses A, T, G and C, while RNA usually uses U in place of T.

structure.text: A context-dependent noun: nitrogenous base here, not a chromosome's bottom end or necessarily a whole nucleotide.

words.whatItDoes: Base identity varies along a nucleic-acid strand, supplying sequence information and pairing specificity.
words.commonConfusion: Bases are not amino acids.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can backbone chemistry remain similar while DNA sequences carry different information?

words.definition: The end/direction associated with the sugar's 5′ carbon in a nucleic-acid strand.

structure.text: Read five-prime, written 5′. The numeral identifies a sugar carbon; the prime distinguishes sugar numbering from base numbering.

words.whatItDoes: The label identifies orientation by the sugar-carbon numbering convention.
words.commonConfusion: It does not mean the fifth nucleotide in a sequence.
words.retrievalPrompt: Label the opposite ends of a strand written 5′-ATGC-3′.

words.definition: The end/direction associated with the sugar's 3′ carbon; polymerases extend a strand at its available 3′ hydroxyl.

structure.text: Read three-prime, written 3′. It marks a sugar-carbon position used to specify strand orientation.

words.whatItDoes: The available terminal hydroxyl is the site where polymerases extend the new chain.
words.commonConfusion: A 3′ end is not a signal that a strand contains three bases.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does adding to the 3′ end produce synthesis described as 5′ to 3′?

words.definition: Rosalind Franklin, whose X-ray diffraction work provided important structural evidence for DNA.

structure.text: Rosalind Franklin is a personal name, not a molecular part or a word-root abbreviation.

words.whatItDoes: Her diffraction work contributed experimental constraints on models of DNA structure.
words.commonConfusion: A structural model is not the same evidence source as the diffraction pattern informing it.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish a DNA diffraction observation from a model built using that evidence.

words.definition: James Watson, who worked with Francis Crick on a model of DNA structure informed by experimental evidence.

structure.text: James Watson is a personal name associated with DNA model building, not a component of DNA.

words.whatItDoes: His collaborative model-building with Crick organized structural evidence into a proposed DNA arrangement.
words.commonConfusion: Model construction did not replace the experimental contributions of other researchers.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why should an account of DNA structure distinguish model builders from the sources of experimental data?

words.definition: Francis Crick, who worked with James Watson on a model of DNA structure informed by experimental evidence.

structure.text: Francis Crick is a personal name associated with DNA model building, not a type of chemical bond.

words.whatItDoes: His collaborative DNA model work helped explain how strand arrangement and pairing could fit available evidence.
words.commonConfusion: A historically important model still depends on observations that constrain and test it.
words.retrievalPrompt: What makes a structural model more scientifically useful than an unconstrained drawing?

words.definition: A method that infers molecular structure from the pattern produced when X-rays scatter through an ordered sample.

structure.text: Diffraction names scattering-related pattern formation; X-ray identifies the radiation used.

words.whatItDoes: Scattering patterns from ordered material constrain molecular spacing and organization.
words.commonConfusion: A diffraction pattern is not a direct ordinary photograph of individual atoms.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does interpreting a diffraction pattern require a structural model?

words.definition: Erwin Chargaff, whose measurements established important base-composition relationships in DNA.

structure.text: Erwin Chargaff is a personal name associated with base-composition findings, not a DNA base.

words.whatItDoes: Base-composition measurements supplied relationships that a double-stranded DNA model needed to explain.
words.commonConfusion: The relationships apply to the appropriate double-stranded sample, not necessarily either strand alone.
words.retrievalPrompt: If double-stranded DNA is 30% A, predict T, G and C under the usual base-pairing model.

words.definition: Able to match through the specified base-pairing relationships, such as A–T and G–C in DNA.

structure.text: An adjective for specific matching relationships. Complementary does not mean identical or parallel.

words.whatItDoes: Specific base-pair rules let one strand specify a partner sequence.
words.commonConfusion: Complementary does not mean identical left-to-right sequence.
words.retrievalPrompt: Write the aligned complementary strand to 5′-AGTC-3′ and label both ends.

words.definition: Describes DNA strands running in opposite 5-prime-to-3-prime directions.

structure.text: Anti- indicates opposing orientation; parallel describes aligned strands running in opposite chemical directions.

words.whatItDoes: Opposite strand directions permit the standard DNA pairing arrangement and shape replication requirements.
words.commonConfusion: Complementary bases alone are insufficient if strand directions are incorrectly labelled.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must the aligned partner to a 5′ to 3′ strand run 3′ to 5′?

words.definition: A noncovalent interaction contributing to the specificity and stability of paired DNA bases.

structure.text: Bond is the interaction; hydrogen identifies the participating atomic feature. It is not the covalent backbone bond.

words.whatItDoes: Interactions between paired bases contribute to pairing specificity and duplex stability.
words.commonConfusion: Hydrogen bonds between bases differ from covalent backbone bonds.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which interactions are separated when DNA strands unzip without cutting their backbones?

words.definition: The connected sugar-phosphate chain of a nucleic-acid strand.

structure.text: A structural metaphor for the repeating chain framework; the sugar-phosphate backbone is not made of paired bases.

words.whatItDoes: Covalent sugar–phosphate connections maintain each strand's continuity and direction.
words.commonConfusion: The backbone does not alternate amino acids and bases.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain why separating two DNA strands need not break each strand into nucleotides.

words.definition: A strand or pattern used to specify a complementary product.

structure.text: Template is a pattern used to guide synthesis; specify which strand is the template in the stated process.

words.whatItDoes: Its sequence guides complementary synthesis of a new nucleic-acid strand.
words.commonConfusion: A template strand and its product do not have identical complementary base identities.
words.retrievalPrompt: Given a template's sequence and direction, what two rules determine the product?

words.definition: An original DNA strand present before the replication event being followed.

structure.text: Parental means pre-existing relative to replication, not inherited exclusively from a male or female parent.

words.whatItDoes: An original strand supplies a template and remains within a daughter duplex after semiconservative replication.
words.commonConfusion: Both parental strands are not retained together in one duplex after normal semiconservative copying.
words.retrievalPrompt: Track the two old strands through one replication round.

words.definition: A newly synthesized DNA strand produced during replication.

structure.text: Daughter means newly synthesized relative to a template; it does not refer to the sex of an organism.

words.whatItDoes: New nucleotides form a complementary partner to a parental template.
words.commonConfusion: A daughter duplex contains one daughter strand, not necessarily two newly synthesized strands.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish a daughter strand from a daughter double-stranded DNA molecule.

words.definition: An enzyme that separates paired DNA strands at a replication fork.

structure.text: The -ase ending marks an enzyme name. Helicase separates paired strands; its name does not make it a DNA-cutting nuclease.

words.whatItDoes: Strand separation exposes templates at the replication fork.
words.commonConfusion: Helicase separates base-paired strands; it does not synthesize their new complements.
words.retrievalPrompt: What replication step becomes unavailable if templates cannot be exposed?

words.definition: A short nucleic-acid strand providing a free 3-prime end for polymerase extension and helping define the copied region.

structure.text: A whole process-related noun for the starting nucleic-acid segment. Priming is preparation for extension.

words.whatItDoes: A short paired starter provides an extendable 3′ end for DNA synthesis.
words.commonConfusion: DNA polymerase generally cannot start an ordinary new chain without an appropriate end.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is a primer needed before DNA polymerase can extend a strand?

words.definition: An enzyme that builds DNA by adding complementary nucleotides to an existing 3-prime end and often proofreads the product.

structure.text: Polymerase is the enzyme name; DNA identifies its product. The -ase ending signals an enzyme.

words.whatItDoes: It adds complementary nucleotides at an existing 3′ end and can correct some incorporation errors.
words.commonConfusion: It does not synthesize one new strand 3′ to 5′ to solve antiparallel geometry.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why do both leading and lagging strands still grow chemically 5′ to 3′?

words.definition: The direction in which a new DNA or RNA strand is extended by adding nucleotides to its 3′ end.

structure.text: The ordered phrase specifies synthesis direction along the growing strand, not movement along the template in the same direction.

words.whatItDoes: New nucleotides extend the growing chain at its 3′ end.
words.commonConfusion: Synthesis direction differs from the direction in which the template is read.
words.retrievalPrompt: Label template-reading and product-synthesis directions during copying.

words.definition: The Y-shaped region where parental DNA strands separate and new DNA strands are synthesized.

structure.text: Fork is a shape metaphor; replication identifies the active DNA-copying junction.

words.whatItDoes: Local strand opening supports synthesis on both exposed templates.
words.commonConfusion: One fork's direction does not change the chemistry of nucleotide addition.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why do opposite template orientations require continuous and discontinuous synthesis at a fork?

words.definition: The new DNA strand synthesized continuously toward an advancing replication fork.

structure.text: Leading modifies strand relative to fork movement; it does not mean the strand has more genes.

words.whatItDoes: Its new strand can extend continuously in the direction of fork advance.
words.commonConfusion: Continuous synthesis does not mean no primer was needed.
words.retrievalPrompt: Relate leading-strand synthesis direction to the moving replication fork.

words.definition: The new DNA strand synthesized discontinuously as Okazaki fragments away from each advancing replication fork.

structure.text: Lagging is relative to fork movement and discontinuous synthesis, not a different polymerase growth direction.

words.whatItDoes: Repeated starts make short segments while maintaining 5′ to 3′ synthesis.
words.commonConfusion: Lagging does not mean DNA polymerase runs chemically backward.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does this strand require repeated fragments rather than one uninterrupted start?

words.definition: A short DNA segment synthesized discontinuously on the lagging strand and later joined by DNA ligase.

structure.text: Okazaki is a personal name; fragment names one short newly synthesized lagging-strand DNA segment.

words.whatItDoes: A short newly synthesized segment is processed and joined into a continuous lagging strand.
words.commonConfusion: A fragment is not a broken piece of the parental template.
words.retrievalPrompt: How do short lagging-strand segments become one continuous daughter strand?

words.definition: An enzyme that seals breaks in a DNA sugar-phosphate backbone by forming phosphodiester bonds.

structure.text: The -ase ending indicates an enzyme. Ligase seals a backbone connection; it does not add complementary bases as a polymerase does.

words.whatItDoes: It seals appropriate backbone nicks by forming covalent phosphodiester connections.
words.commonConfusion: Ligase does not replace complementary base pairing or synthesize a whole new strand.
words.retrievalPrompt: What remains to be joined after neighbouring DNA fragments have been synthesized and processed?

words.definition: Detection and correction of some newly incorporated nucleotide errors during DNA replication.

structure.text: A checking metaphor for correction during synthesis, not conscious reading or a guarantee of error-free DNA.

words.whatItDoes: Some polymerases detect and remove misincorporated nucleotides during copying.
words.commonConfusion: Proofreading is not perfect and does not prevent every mutation.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can mutations still arise despite proofreading?

words.definition: A change in DNA sequence that can create a new allele; whether it reaches offspring depends on the cell lineage and reproduction.

structure.text: Mutation is the change noun; mutant and mutated describe the resulting variant. The name does not specify harm.

words.whatItDoes: A sequence change can create a new allele and may persist through descendant cells.
words.commonConfusion: Not every mutation changes a protein or enters the next organismal generation.
words.retrievalPrompt: What determines whether a sequence change in one cell can be inherited by offspring?

words.definition: A stated expected result that would follow if a proposed explanation and its assumptions were correct.

structure.text: Prediction is the anticipated observation; experimental ties it to a defined test and conditions.

words.whatItDoes: An explanation yields an expected observation under stated conditions that can be checked.
words.commonConfusion: A prediction is not evidence that the outcome has already occurred.
words.retrievalPrompt: What result would distinguish semiconservative copying from a model retaining both old strands together?

words.definition: A DNA region where transcription machinery assembles to initiate transcription of a gene.

structure.text: A whole technical noun for a regulatory DNA region. It is not the protein enzyme that synthesizes RNA.

words.whatItDoes: Transcription machinery assembles at an appropriate DNA region to initiate RNA synthesis.
words.commonConfusion: A promoter is not the translated start codon.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could changing a promoter alter RNA amount without changing a protein-coding sequence?

words.definition: The DNA strand read by RNA polymerase to synthesize a complementary RNA transcript.

structure.text: Strand is the DNA chain; template specifies the chain used for a particular transcription event.

words.whatItDoes: RNA polymerase reads this strand to make an antiparallel complementary RNA.
words.commonConfusion: The template is not the DNA strand that simply matches the RNA sequence.
words.retrievalPrompt: Transcribe 3′-TACGGA-5′ and label the RNA ends.

words.definition: The DNA strand whose sequence matches the RNA transcript except that DNA has thymine where RNA has uracil.

structure.text: Coding specifies correspondence with the RNA sequence using T instead of U; it does not mean polymerase reads this strand as template.

words.whatItDoes: Its 5′ to 3′ sequence corresponds to the RNA, with T replaced by U.
words.commonConfusion: It is not the strand directly read as the template for that transcript.
words.retrievalPrompt: Given coding DNA 5′-ATGCCA-3′, write the corresponding RNA.

words.definition: An enzyme that uses a DNA template to synthesize a complementary RNA molecule.

structure.text: RNA identifies the synthesized polymer; polymerase names the enzyme rather than the DNA region it binds.

words.whatItDoes: It builds RNA from a DNA template using complementary nucleotides.
words.commonConfusion: RNA synthesis does not convert or consume the DNA template into RNA.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can one DNA region be transcribed repeatedly?

words.definition: Ribonucleic acid: a molecule related to DNA whose chemical units usually use U instead of T; different RNAs carry information, help assemble proteins or carry out other cellular functions.

structure.text: Initialism for ribonucleic acid. Ribo- refers to ribose; RNA is not an abbreviation for a protein.

words.whatItDoes: Different RNA forms carry coding information, act as adaptors or contribute structural and catalytic functions.
words.commonConfusion: RNA is not solely a temporary messenger for proteins.
words.retrievalPrompt: Name two non-messenger roles that RNA can perform.

words.definition: The RNA base that pairs with adenine in the usual transcription model.

structure.text: A whole chemical name for an RNA base; U is its sequence symbol, not a separate nucleotide type name.

words.whatItDoes: It serves as the usual RNA pairing partner for adenine.
words.commonConfusion: Uracil replaces thymine in the standard RNA sequence, not every DNA base.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which RNA base pairs with A on a DNA template?

words.definition: Specific hydrogen-bond pairing of adenine with thymine or uracil and guanine with cytosine.

structure.text: The noun formed from complementary; it names the matching relationship between bases rather than strand direction.

words.whatItDoes: Specific pairing constrains matching nucleic-acid sequences.
words.commonConfusion: Complementary and identical sequences are not interchangeable.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish the complementary template relationship from the coding-strand match to RNA.

words.definition: An RNA molecule carrying a coding sequence from DNA transcription to a ribosome for translation.

structure.text: m stands for messenger; RNA stands for ribonucleic acid. The mixed-case abbreviation identifies a functional RNA class.

words.whatItDoes: Its coding sequence is read by ribosomes to specify polypeptide sequence.
words.commonConfusion: An mRNA codon is not an amino acid or a tRNA anticodon.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace the information carried by mRNA between transcription and translation.

words.definition: A transcribed segment removed from a pre-mRNA during RNA splicing.

structure.text: A whole technical name for a transcribed region removed in the splicing context; intronic is the adjective.

words.whatItDoes: A transcribed region is removed during processing of the relevant pre-mRNA.
words.commonConfusion: Introns are transcribed even though they are removed from the mature RNA.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can mature mRNA be shorter than the initial transcript?

words.definition: A transcript segment retained in a mature RNA after splicing, though not every exon segment is protein-coding.

structure.text: A whole technical name for a region retained in mature RNA after splicing; exonic does not necessarily mean protein-coding.

words.whatItDoes: Retained transcript regions are joined into mature RNA after splicing.
words.commonConfusion: Not all retained exon sequence is translated into amino acids.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can an exon include sequence outside the protein-coding region?

words.definition: Removal of introns and joining of exons from a pre-mRNA transcript.

structure.text: An joining/editing metaphor: splicing removes specified RNA regions and joins retained regions.

words.whatItDoes: Processing removes introns and connects retained exons.
words.commonConfusion: Splicing edits the RNA transcript, not automatically the original DNA sequence.
words.retrievalPrompt: What changes and what remains unchanged when an intron is removed from pre-mRNA?

words.definition: Specific hydrogen-bond pairing of adenine with thymine or uracil and guanine with cytosine.

structure.text: Pairing is the interaction; base identifies the chemical units involved, not whole chromosomes.

words.whatItDoes: Pairing rules support replication, transcription and codon–anticodon recognition.
words.commonConfusion: Pairing needs appropriate direction labels as well as matching letters.
words.retrievalPrompt: Write an antiparallel RNA partner to a short specified DNA template.

words.definition: The stated orientation of a process or strand; nucleic-acid answers require 5′ and 3′ labels.

structure.text: A relationship requiring endpoints: in sequence problems write 5′ and 3′ rather than only left and right.

words.whatItDoes: Explicit 5′ and 3′ labels distinguish how a strand is read and synthesized.
words.commonConfusion: Reversing a written sequence is not the same as complementing it.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can an unlabelled correct-looking base string still be an ambiguous transcription answer?

words.definition: The amount of a specified RNA present in a sample at a stated time; it is influenced by production and breakdown.

structure.text: Abundance means amount present; RNA identifies the measured molecule, not automatically the synthesis rate.

words.whatItDoes: The amount present reflects both synthesis and breakdown over time.
words.commonConfusion: More RNA does not alone prove faster transcription if degradation also changes.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could RNA abundance rise without a change in transcription rate?

words.definition: A three-nucleotide mRNA sequence that specifies an amino acid or a translation start or stop signal.

structure.text: Codon is the triplet-unit noun; codons is plural. A codon belongs to the read mRNA sequence, unlike a tRNA anticodon.

words.whatItDoes: A triplet in the coding frame specifies an amino acid or translation signal.
words.commonConfusion: A codon chart is read using the mRNA orientation, not an unconverted DNA template.
words.retrievalPrompt: Before using a codon chart, what sequence and direction must be established?

words.definition: The grouping of an RNA coding sequence into consecutive three-nucleotide codons.

structure.text: Frame is the grouping convention; reading specifies successive triplets from a selected start position.

words.whatItDoes: Starting position groups nucleotides into successive nonoverlapping triplets.
words.commonConfusion: The same nucleotide string can yield different triplets if the starting position changes.
words.retrievalPrompt: Show how shifting the start by one base changes codon grouping.

words.definition: A codon, usually AUG, that establishes the translation reading frame and specifies methionine.

structure.text: Start modifies codon by its initiation role; not every occurrence of the same triplet serves as an initiation site.

words.whatItDoes: The recognized initiation codon establishes the translated frame and begins the chain.
words.commonConfusion: Not every AUG anywhere in an RNA necessarily initiates translation.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must initiation context be considered rather than translating from every AUG?

words.definition: An mRNA codon that recruits a release factor and ends translation rather than specifying an amino acid.

structure.text: Stop names the termination signal; the codon does not encode a special stop amino acid.

words.whatItDoes: It signals termination through release-factor recognition rather than specifying an amino acid.
words.commonConfusion: Stop is not an additional amino acid placed at the chain end.
words.retrievalPrompt: How does decoding a stop codon differ from decoding an amino-acid codon?

words.definition: An adaptor RNA carrying a specific amino acid and an anticodon that pairs with an mRNA codon.

structure.text: t stands for transfer; RNA is ribonucleic acid. This abbreviation identifies the adaptor RNA class.

words.whatItDoes: It connects codon recognition to delivery of an amino acid during translation.
words.commonConfusion: An anticodon match does not itself attach the correct amino acid; charging is a separate step.
words.retrievalPrompt: How does tRNA link an mRNA triplet to a growing amino-acid chain?

words.definition: A three-nucleotide sequence on tRNA that pairs with a complementary mRNA codon.

structure.text: Anti- marks the complementary counterpart to the codon; the anticodon is on tRNA, not mRNA.

words.whatItDoes: Its antiparallel pairing with a codon helps position the matching charged tRNA.
words.commonConfusion: The anticodon is on tRNA, not on the DNA template.
words.retrievalPrompt: Write the aligned anticodon for 5′-AUG-3′ and label its direction.

words.definition: An RNA-protein complex that reads mRNA codons and catalyzes polypeptide synthesis.

structure.text: A whole organelle/complex name; ribosomal is the adjective. A ribosome contains RNA and proteins, not only ribose.

words.whatItDoes: It coordinates mRNA reading and catalyzes peptide-bond formation using its RNA–protein structure.
words.commonConfusion: A ribosome does not transcribe DNA into mRNA.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which part of gene expression requires the ribosome rather than RNA polymerase?

words.definition: One of the small chemical building blocks joined into a protein chain.

structure.text: A compound chemical name; amino and acid refer to characteristic groups, not separate molecules in a polypeptide.

words.whatItDoes: Amino acids join through peptide bonds and their side chains influence folding and interactions.
words.commonConfusion: Amino acids are not the bases read in a codon chart.
words.retrievalPrompt: How does a sequence of RNA bases specify a different type of molecular sequence?

words.definition: The covalent bond linking amino acids in a polypeptide.

structure.text: Bond is the connection; peptide identifies the covalent linkage joining amino-acid residues.

words.whatItDoes: A covalent linkage joins neighbouring amino acids in the growing chain.
words.commonConfusion: Peptide bonds are not the hydrogen bonds pairing DNA bases.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which bond must form to extend a polypeptide by one amino acid?

words.definition: The assembly and starting stage of a process, such as translation at an appropriate start site.

structure.text: The beginning-stage noun; initiation in translation differs from initiation of replication or transcription.

words.whatItDoes: Assembly at the appropriate start establishes the components and frame for translation.
words.commonConfusion: Initiation is not merely finding any triplet that resembles a start codon.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must the ribosome establish the correct start position before elongation?

words.definition: The stage in which a growing RNA or polypeptide chain is extended.

structure.text: A process noun for lengthening; in translation it is the polypeptide that grows.

words.whatItDoes: Repeated cycles extend the chain using the specified template or codon sequence.
words.commonConfusion: RNA elongation and polypeptide elongation use different monomers and machinery.
words.retrievalPrompt: Contrast the material added during transcription elongation and translation elongation.

words.definition: The ending stage of a process, such as release of a polypeptide at a stop codon.

structure.text: The ending-stage noun; termination of translation does not mean destruction of the completed protein.

words.whatItDoes: A defined signal ends the process and releases its product.
words.commonConfusion: Transcription termination and translation termination are not the same molecular event.
words.retrievalPrompt: What is released when translation terminates at a stop codon?

words.definition: A protein that helps terminate translation at a stop codon and release the polypeptide.

structure.text: Factor names a participating protein; release specifies its role at a stop codon.

words.whatItDoes: It recognizes a termination signal and promotes release of the completed chain.
words.commonConfusion: A release factor is not a tRNA carrying a stop amino acid.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does a stop codon require a release factor rather than an aminoacyl-tRNA?

words.definition: A chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds that can fold or combine to form a functional protein.

structure.text: Poly- means many; peptide concerns linked amino-acid residues. A polypeptide is not a chain of nucleotides.

words.whatItDoes: The amino-acid chain can fold and associate with other components to form a functioning protein.
words.commonConfusion: A newly made chain need not immediately be a fully functional protein.
words.retrievalPrompt: What may need to happen between chain synthesis and biological function?

words.definition: The process by which a polypeptide adopts a three-dimensional structure influenced by sequence and conditions.

structure.text: A shape-change process noun; protein folding concerns three-dimensional conformation, not DNA base pairing.

words.whatItDoes: Sequence and cellular conditions guide formation of a three-dimensional arrangement.
words.commonConfusion: The same primary sequence does not guarantee unchanged structure under every condition.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could altered temperature disrupt protein function without changing DNA sequence?

words.definition: The biological role of a protein, depending on its structure, location, interactions and regulation.

structure.text: Function is the biological activity; protein names the molecule whose structure enables it.

words.whatItDoes: Structure, localization and interactions allow the protein to perform its role.
words.commonConfusion: A sequence change cannot establish a functional effect without considering context or evidence.
words.retrievalPrompt: What evidence would test whether an amino-acid substitution changes enzyme function?

words.definition: Replacement of one nucleotide or chromosome segment with another.

structure.text: Substitution names replacement: one sequence unit is exchanged for another, unlike insertion or deletion.

words.whatItDoes: Replacing a sequence unit may change coding or regulation depending on its position.
words.commonConfusion: A single-base substitution does not usually shift the reading frame.
words.retrievalPrompt: Compare possible silent, missense and nonsense outcomes of one coding-base replacement.

words.definition: Addition of one or more nucleotides or of a chromosome segment.

structure.text: Insertion names addition into a sequence. An insertion is not always a frameshift; its length and location matter.

words.whatItDoes: Added nucleotides can change sequence length and, in some coding contexts, codon grouping.
words.commonConfusion: Not every insertion causes a frameshift; size and location matter.
words.retrievalPrompt: Contrast adding one nucleotide with adding three within a coding region.

words.definition: Loss of one or more nucleotides or of a chromosome segment.

structure.text: Deletion names removal from a sequence. The word alone does not specify the number of removed bases.

words.whatItDoes: Loss of sequence can remove information or alter downstream reading depending on size and position.
words.commonConfusion: A deletion outside a coding region need not produce a frameshift.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does deleting three coding nucleotides differ from deleting one?

words.definition: A reading-frame change caused by insertion or deletion of nucleotides not in a multiple of three within a coding region.

structure.text: A compound of frame and shift: the downstream triplet grouping changes, not simply any sequence base.

words.whatItDoes: A non-triplet coding insertion or deletion regroups downstream codons.
words.commonConfusion: A frameshift is not just any change in one amino acid.
words.retrievalPrompt: Show how a one-base deletion changes the codon groups after its position.

words.definition: A coding substitution that leaves the encoded amino acid unchanged in the specified frame; other effects are still possible.

structure.text: A conventional mutation-effect label; silent for amino-acid sequence does not guarantee no biological consequence.

words.whatItDoes: The altered codon still specifies the same amino acid in the stated frame.
words.commonConfusion: Same amino acid does not prove absolutely no effect on expression or processing.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can two different codons encode the same amino acid without changing the reading frame?

words.definition: A coding-sequence change that substitutes one amino acid for another in a protein.

structure.text: A technical substitution-effect label: the encoded amino acid changes. It does not describe the organism's intentions.

words.whatItDoes: A coding change substitutes an amino acid that may alter structure or function.
words.commonConfusion: A missense change is not automatically harmful or a premature stop.
words.retrievalPrompt: What additional evidence is needed to judge the effect of one amino-acid replacement?

words.definition: A coding-sequence change that converts an amino-acid codon into a stop codon.

structure.text: A technical label for a change creating a premature stop signal, not meaningless DNA.

words.whatItDoes: A coding substitution creates an early stop signal that can shorten the translated product.
words.commonConfusion: Nonsense does not mean random meaningless DNA throughout the gene.
words.retrievalPrompt: How does creating a stop codon midway through a coding region affect the expected chain?

words.definition: A DNA change that affects when, where or how much a gene is expressed.

structure.text: Regulatory specifies a role in controlling expression; mutation names the sequence change.

words.whatItDoes: Changed control sequences can alter the amount, timing or location of expression.
words.commonConfusion: A mutation need not alter the protein-coding sequence to affect phenotype.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could two cells make different amounts of the same protein after a regulatory change?

words.definition: A mutation arising in a non-gamete cell lineage that can affect descendant cells but is usually not inherited by offspring.

structure.text: Somatic identifies body-cell context; mutation describes a DNA change rather than a whole new organism.

words.whatItDoes: The change can spread through descendants of the altered body cell.
words.commonConfusion: A body-cell mutation is not normally transmitted through gametes in the animal model.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can a somatic mutation affect a tissue without appearing in offspring?

words.definition: A mutation in a gamete-producing lineage that can be transmitted to offspring.

structure.text: Germ-line locates the change in a lineage contributing to gametes, not an infectious germ.

words.whatItDoes: A change in a gamete-producing lineage can enter the next generation if transmitted.
words.commonConfusion: Presence in the germ line does not guarantee that every offspring inherits it.
words.retrievalPrompt: What transmission step determines whether a germ-line variant reaches a particular offspring?

words.definition: The idea that a mutation does not arise because the organism anticipates a useful outcome.

structure.text: Random qualifies origin relative to adaptive need; it does not claim every genome position has the same mutation rate.

words.whatItDoes: Mutations arise without anticipating which change would be useful in a future environment.
words.commonConfusion: Random with respect to need does not imply equal mutation probabilities at every site.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does later selection for a variant not show that need caused that variant to arise?

words.definition: Change in representation associated with differences in survival or reproductive success under stated conditions.

structure.text: Selection is differential survival or reproduction in this context, not an organism choosing a needed mutation.

words.whatItDoes: Differences in survival or reproduction change representation of existing variants under given conditions.
words.commonConfusion: Selection does not intentionally manufacture the needed mutation.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish the origin of a resistance variant from its later increase under selection.

words.definition: An agent that can increase the chance of changes to genetic material.

structure.text: A whole technical noun for a mutation-inducing agent; mutagenic is its adjective.

words.whatItDoes: Exposure can increase the probability of genetic changes through interactions with genetic material or its maintenance.
words.commonConfusion: Increased probability is not a guarantee that every exposed cell mutates.
words.retrievalPrompt: What comparison would test whether an exposure increases mutation frequency?

words.definition: The amount of an agent delivered or received, with its units and exposure conditions stated.

structure.text: Dose is an amount under specified exposure conditions; it is distinct from risk or mutation count.

words.whatItDoes: A stated amount and exposure context make treatment comparisons interpretable.
words.commonConfusion: A substance name without amount, duration or delivery conditions is not a complete exposure description.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which units and conditions would you record when comparing two experimental doses?

words.definition: A comparison condition or regulated variable used to make an investigation interpretable.

structure.text: A comparison condition in an experiment; do not confuse it with a regulatory controller in a biological system.

words.whatItDoes: Comparison conditions or held variables help separate a treatment effect from other differences.
words.commonConfusion: A no-treatment group alone does not control unequal handling.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why should treated and comparison samples otherwise undergo the same procedure?

words.definition: A transparent description of limits in measurement, sampling, models, evidence, or prediction.

structure.text: Un- negates certainty; the noun names limits on confidence or precision, not automatic invalidity.

words.whatItDoes: Explicit limits communicate how strongly a result supports a conclusion.
words.commonConfusion: Uncertainty is not an excuse to discard all evidence or claim all explanations equally likely.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish measurement uncertainty from uncertainty about the correct inheritance model.

words.definition: An enzyme that recognizes a particular DNA sequence and cuts the phosphodiester backbone at or near that site.

structure.text: Enzyme is the biological catalyst; restriction identifies this DNA-cleaving enzyme class.

words.whatItDoes: Sequence recognition directs cutting of the DNA backbone at defined sites.
words.commonConfusion: It cuts the backbone, not merely the bonds between paired bases.
words.retrievalPrompt: How does sequence specificity help predict fragment lengths after a restriction digest?

words.definition: A specific DNA sequence bound and cut by a particular restriction endonuclease.

structure.text: Site is a location; recognition specifies the sequence feature recognized by the molecule or enzyme.

words.whatItDoes: Its sequence determines where a particular enzyme can bind and cut under suitable conditions.
words.commonConfusion: Different restriction enzymes need not recognize the same sequence.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could a base substitution remove a restriction site without changing total DNA length?

words.definition: A single-stranded DNA overhang produced by staggered cutting and capable of complementary base pairing.

structure.text: Sticky is a pairing metaphor; end names a single-stranded overhang capable of complementary pairing.

words.whatItDoes: An exposed overhang pairs with a compatible complementary end before covalent joining.
words.commonConfusion: Compatible pairing alone does not seal the DNA backbone.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why are both complementary ends and ligase relevant when joining fragments?

words.definition: A DNA molecule used to carry and replicate or express inserted genetic material in a host cell.

structure.text: A context-dependent noun: a DNA carrier here, not a geometric arrow or disease-transmitting animal.

words.whatItDoes: A carrier construct enables introduced DNA to be maintained or expressed in a host.
words.commonConfusion: A vector is not the inserted gene itself.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish the carrier backbone from the inserted coding sequence in a plasmid construct.

words.definition: A usually circular DNA molecule that replicates separately from a cell's main chromosome and can serve as a biotechnology vector.

structure.text: A whole molecule name; plasmid-borne describes information carried on it. The name does not imply viral DNA.

words.whatItDoes: Independent replication can maintain a small DNA molecule carrying selected genes or inserts.
words.commonConfusion: Not all plasmids automatically express every inserted sequence.
words.retrievalPrompt: What features beyond a DNA insert are needed for the intended host use?

words.definition: The DNA segment placed into a vector or other specified DNA construct.

structure.text: A noun for the DNA segment placed into a vector; insertion names the act or sequence change.

words.whatItDoes: The chosen DNA segment adds a sequence to the construct for the intended study or expression task.
words.commonConfusion: An insert's presence does not prove its orientation or expression is correct.
words.retrievalPrompt: What check would distinguish having an insert from having the intended insert in the intended orientation?

words.definition: Polymerase chain reaction; a laboratory method that uses primers and repeated temperature cycles to amplify a selected DNA region.

structure.text: Initialism for polymerase chain reaction. Chain reaction describes repeated amplification, not protein translation.

words.whatItDoes: Repeated denaturation, primer annealing and extension amplify a primer-bounded region.
words.commonConfusion: PCR amplifies DNA; it does not itself establish a sequence's biological function.
words.retrievalPrompt: How do primer-binding sites determine which region is amplified?

words.definition: A method that separates charged molecules through a gel, commonly resolving DNA fragments mainly by length.

structure.text: Electro- concerns electricity and -phoresis movement; gel specifies the medium through which charged fragments migrate.

words.whatItDoes: Charged fragments move through a matrix, with length affecting migration under the specified conditions.
words.commonConfusion: A DNA band's position does not reveal its full base sequence.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can equal-length DNA fragments share a band despite different sequences?

words.definition: The length of a DNA fragment, commonly measured in base pairs.

structure.text: Size here is usually sequence length in bases or base pairs, not the darkness of a gel band.

words.whatItDoes: Length in bases or base pairs allows comparisons with a size reference.
words.commonConfusion: Size is not the same as DNA amount in a band.
words.retrievalPrompt: Distinguish the information suggested by band position and band intensity.

words.definition: A set of DNA fragments of known sizes used as a gel reference.

structure.text: A visual metaphor for a set of reference fragments; its known sizes support comparisons on a gel.

words.whatItDoes: Known fragment lengths provide comparison points for estimating sample fragment size.
words.commonConfusion: A ladder is a reference, not another unknown sample.
words.retrievalPrompt: How would you estimate the size of a band falling between two ladder bands?

words.definition: DNA contained in the nucleus, including the chromosomes used in ordinary nuclear inheritance models.

structure.text: Nuclear identifies the cellular compartment, not atomic nuclei or every DNA molecule in the cell.

words.whatItDoes: Chromosomal sequences in the nucleus supply the nuclear inheritance patterns analysed in ordinary crosses.
words.commonConfusion: Not all cellular DNA is nuclear.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why may a nuclear inheritance model fail to describe a mitochondrial marker?

words.definition: DNA contained in mitochondria; its inheritance pattern differs from that of nuclear chromosomes in many organisms.

structure.text: Mitochondrial is the adjective from mitochondrion; DNA identifies the organelle's genetic material.

words.whatItDoes: Mitochondrial sequences supply additional genetic information with organelle-specific transmission patterns.
words.commonConfusion: Maternal inheritance is common in the studied examples, not a universal rule for every organism.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must the organism's transmission pattern be specified before interpreting a mitochondrial pedigree?

words.definition: DNA contained in chloroplasts, useful alongside other sequences when comparing related organisms.

structure.text: Chloroplast identifies the organelle carrying the DNA, not a green base or a chlorophyll gene alone.

words.whatItDoes: Plastid sequences provide an additional source of inherited markers in photosynthetic lineages.
words.commonConfusion: A chloroplast sequence is not necessarily inherited like a nuclear autosomal locus.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can comparing chloroplast and nuclear markers provide different lineage information?

words.definition: An analysis of appropriately aligned nucleotide sequences to identify similarities and differences.

structure.text: Comparison names the analysis; sequence specifies the ordered units rather than overall organism appearance.

words.whatItDoes: Aligned homologous positions reveal similarities and differences relevant to the comparison question.
words.commonConfusion: Equal sequence similarity is not alone proof of one unique evolutionary history.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must sequences be appropriately aligned before counting differences?

words.definition: An approach intended to treat a condition by altering genetic material or its delivery/expression in relevant cells.

structure.text: Therapy names a treatment approach; gene specifies intervention involving genetic material, not guaranteed cure.

words.whatItDoes: A proposed intervention changes genetic material or its expression in relevant cells to address a condition.
words.commonConfusion: Changing some target cells does not imply correction in every cell or guaranteed benefit.
words.retrievalPrompt: What delivery and target-cell limitations must accompany a gene-therapy claim?

words.definition: Analysis of genetic material to investigate a specified variant or question, with limits determined by the method.

structure.text: Testing is the analysis process; genetic identifies the information investigated rather than a diagnosis by itself.

words.whatItDoes: A chosen assay answers a specific sequence or chromosome question within its detection limits.
words.commonConfusion: A negative result does not exclude variants outside the method's scope.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must a genetic-test report state which variants or changes it can detect?

words.definition: The possibility and potential consequence of an adverse outcome under specified conditions.

structure.text: Risk combines a possible adverse outcome with its chance or uncertainty; it is not certainty that harm will occur.

words.whatItDoes: It combines the possibility of an adverse outcome with its consequences in a specified context.
words.commonConfusion: Risk is not certainty, and an unspecified denominator makes a probability hard to interpret.
words.retrievalPrompt: What population, interval and outcome must be named to make a risk estimate interpretable?

words.definition: Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate during a cell division.

structure.text: Non- negates disjunction, separation. The whole term names a failure of the specified chromosomes or chromatids to separate.

words.whatItDoes: Failure of the appropriate separation distributes chromosome material unevenly between products.
words.commonConfusion: It can involve homologues or sisters, so the division stage matters.
words.retrievalPrompt: How do first- and second-meiotic-division failures yield different product patterns?

words.definition: Asexual cell reproduction in which one cell copies its genetic material and divides into two cells.

structure.text: Binary means two; fission means splitting. The phrase names division into two, not mitosis in bacteria.

words.whatItDoes: Copying and partitioning genetic material precede division into two descendant cells.
words.commonConfusion: Binary fission is reproduction; DNA exchange between two existing bacteria is not the same event.
words.retrievalPrompt: Contrast the change in cell number during binary fission and conjugation.

words.definition: Transfer of DNA from a donor bacterium to a recipient through direct cell contact; transfer itself does not make an additional cell.

structure.text: Bacterial identifies the organisms; conjugation names contact-mediated DNA transfer, not gamete fusion.

words.whatItDoes: Direct contact allows DNA transfer between existing donor and recipient cells.
words.commonConfusion: Transfer does not itself create an additional bacterium.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is conjugation genetic exchange rather than reproduction by cell division?

words.definition: A cloning method that transfers a body-cell nucleus into an oocyte whose nucleus has been removed.

structure.text: Somatic-cell identifies the donor-cell type, nuclear identifies the transferred material, and transfer names relocation into an enucleated egg.

words.whatItDoes: A somatic nucleus supplies nuclear genetic material to an enucleated oocyte for a cloning procedure.
words.commonConfusion: Nuclear similarity does not mean identical mitochondrial DNA or developmental environment.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which genetic contribution can come from the oocyte even after its nucleus is removed?
